Carranza gets a short, keen sketch of his own near the end. Mexican nights of song and rite close Reed’s vivid report.
48286-mogreb-el-acksa-a-journey-in-moroc:
Mogreb-el-Acksa is a journey in Morocco by Cunninghame Graham. William Heinemann first published it in 1898. A revised edition, issued by Duckworth in 1921, is the text at hand. A Moorish saying about the moon Sohail stands as its motto.

Graham dedicates the book to Haj Mohammed, his travelling companion of many journeys. The dedication jokes, darkly, about the temptation of lonely places. More than once, it suggests, his guide might have won paradise by killing an unbeliever. Yet Graham swears he would trust the man even on the road to Mecca. The first chapter opens in the harbour of Tangier in October. Long rollers set in under a cloudy sky as the narrative begins. Inside the harbour, lamps draw a gleaming horseshoe of light on the dark water. The book became a classic of Moroccan travel in English.
48367-birds-and-all-nature-vol-7-no-3-ma:
Birds and All Nature for March 1900 is volume seven, number three of a nature magazine. Its pages were illustrated by colour photography, the masthead boasts. Twenty six items fill the contents. The English Sparrow opens the number with a dialect poem. The peacock, the song of the lark, and a herald of spring follow. The willow ptarmigan and Steller's jay take their turns.

Animal pets in school and taming birds address young readers directly. The sycamore warbler, the ruddy duck, and the muskrat continue the animals. Linen fabrics, the poppy, and the primrose vary the natural history. Sponges and common minerals close the scientific run. An egret's young and a piece called The Young Naturalist end the list. Such magazines brought field study into parlours and classrooms. Verse, anecdote, and fact shared every number.
48579-birds-and-nature-vol-08-no-4-novem:
Birds and Nature for November 1900 is Volume Eight Number Four of a monthly magazine shown with color photos. The issue holds poems, short pieces, and nature notes. A sonnet for November by William Cullen Bryant opens the issue. The front list runs from page 145 to page 188.

Pieces cover the Western Willet, fall bird flights, bantams, and the Buffle-Head duck. Other pieces treat the American Eared Grebe, the spread of fishes, and the Louisiana Tanager. Moths, ants, the prong-horned antelope, and plant care get space too. One piece faults the use of bird plumes in fashion. The mix suits home readers who like close facts about wild life.
48606-birds-and-nature-vol-08-no-5-decem:
Birds and Nature, volume eight, number five, is a magazine for December 1900. Colour photography illustrates its bird and nature studies for readers. Contents open with a poem, December, at page 193 of the issue. The western horned owl and a poem, The Owl, follow in order. The long crested jay and the sunrise serenade fill the next pages.

A victim of circumstances and the fulvous tree duck come after that. How the swifts came to build in Aunt Dorothy's chimney delights children. The red breasted sapsucker, a white table in the woods, follow. Cecropia and promethea moths and a plea for protection close it. Carnivorous plants, maple leaves, and may apple end the number.
48892-marriage-with-a-deceased-wife-s-si:
Marriage with a Deceased Wife Sister is a theological letter printed at London and Oxford in 1869. Its author is Mayow, rector of South Heighton cum Tarring Neville in Sussex. The letter goes to Lord Hatherley, lord high chancellor of England at the time. A verse of Leviticus stands at the centre of the case the letter argues.

That verse is weighed beside the old law of the levirate in Hebrew practice. The question was a live one in Victorian England, where such marriages were barred. A second edition shows the debate drew readers enough to warrant fresh print. Parish clergy and lawyers alike followed this church law fight with close care.
48984-the-heart-line-a-drama-of-san-fran:
Gelett Burgess's The Heart Line, a drama of San Francisco, was published by Grosset and Dunlap under a 1907 Bobbs-Merrill copyright, with pictures by Lester Ralph. Burgess had written The White Cat and Vivette before it. A dedication to Maysie, who knew the people and loved the place, keeps the memory of the city that was. Palmistry drives the plot: the heart line of the title is read in hands.

The contents name the palmist and Fancy Gray first, then the spider's nest, the weaving of the web, a materializing seance, and Fancy Gray's acceptance. The prologue goes back to 1877, to the Siskiyou House, a third-class hotel fallen to a cheap tenement. Its rooms were known to the police as a resort of counterfeiters and sharpers, and two of them held Madam Grant.
49225-bandelier-national-monument-new-me:
Bandelier National Monument, New Mexico, by Kittridge A Wing, is handbook number twenty-three of the National Park Service. It was printed at Washington in 1955 and reprinted in 1961, priced at twenty-five cents. Fine canyon and mesa land west of the Rio Grande holds the ruins it guards.

Farm folk of the Pajarito Plateau throve there for some 300 years from the 1200s on. By 1540, when Coronado came, they had begun to leave for the Rio Grande. Pages treat the great ruins in turn, Tyuonyi, Talus House, and Long House. More treat kivas, a rite cave, stone lions, and a painted cave. Food, dress, faith, and the wild scene fill the rest. Guests get a full guide to cliff homes of the old Pueblos.
49314-six-months-in-mexico:
Nellie Bly wrote Six Months in Mexico, issued in New York in 1888. Bly was known for Ten Days in a Mad House. She gives the book to George A Madden of the Pittsburg Dispatch, for his never-failing kindness. Contents run to thirty-seven chapters, from Adieu to the United States to Princess Josefa de Yturbide.

Bly left Pittsburgh one winter night with her mother, a few months after becoming a newspaper woman. Too impatient for usual women's duties, she chose to travel as a correspondent. Three days out, snow gave way to summer leaves and balmy air. She watched women plowing while their husbands sat on fences smoking. Later chapters treat Mexico City, bull-fights, the floating gardens, and Chapultepec castle.
49760-the-adventures-of-hernan-cortes-th:
The author of Uncle Philip's Conversations wrote a life of Hernan Cortes for the young, published at New York in 1843. It forms the fourth volume of a library for his young countrymen. A note says he has kept out references to authorities, as unsuited to a book for boys, but believes every statement can be backed.

His materials are the old Spanish historians, Herrera, Bernal Diaz, and Solis among them, with Cortes's own letters. The contents run from the boy's birth and his lazy spell at Salamanca at fourteen, through disappointments, to Hispaniola in 1504 and the conquest of Cuba under Velasquez. A story of real life stranger than romance, the dedication calls it.
50620-vagabond-life-in-mexico:
Gabriel Ferry, seven years a resident of the country, sketches Mexican low life in Vagabond Life in Mexico, published at New York by Harper and Brothers in 1856. Eight tales make the volume, opening with Perico the Mexican vagabond and Fray Serapio the Franciscan monk. Don Tadeo Cristobal, the thieves' lawyer of Mexico, the miners of Rayas and Captain Don Blas with his silver convoy follow.

Perico's first chapter climbs a cathedral tower at sunset to survey the city. Popocatapetl and Iztaczihuatl rise snow-covered to the south, and the palace of Chapultepec stands westward above its ancient cedar forest.
51238-the-pride-of-jennico-being-a-memoi:
Pride of Jennico is a novel framed as the memoir of Captain Basil Jennico. Agnes and Egerton Castle wrote it, and Macmillan issued it in 1899. Rights pages date the work to 1897 and 1898 in print runs. The memoir purports to begin at the Castle of Tollendhal in Moravia. Its date inside the tale is late in the year 1771.

A great storm frames that start, with the captain in stress of mind. Part one runs through Jennico's memoir in chapter after chapter of peril. Moravia, old houses, and a proud name set the scene for romance. Readers of that day loved tales of honour, swords, and secret pasts. The Castles gave them a swaggering captain with a troubled soul.
51525-the-influence-of-darwin-on-philoso:
The Influence of Darwin on Philosophy, and other essays, is a book by John Dewey, professor of philosophy at Columbia University. Henry Holt and Company published it at New York in 1910. The title essay argues that the Origin of Species marked an age in thought, not in natural science alone. The very joining of the words origin and species, Dewey says, was a revolt in ideas.

For two thousand years, thought about nature and knowledge prized the fixed and final, treating change as a flaw. Darwin's book broke that temper. The other essays treat nature and its good, sense and morals, the trial theory of knowledge, and a short catechism on truth.
5246-modern-french-philosophy-a-study-of:
J. Alexander Gunn's Modern French Philosophy, first published in 1922 with a foreword by Henri Bergson, studies French thought since Auguste Comte. Chapters trace the main currents since 1851, then turn to science, freedom, progress, ethics, and religion, with a comparative table to help readers follow schools and thinkers.

Gunn, a lecturer in psychology at Liverpool, wrote for English readers who wanted a map of a rich philosophical tradition. The book offers a clear survey of French philosophy from the Revolution's aftermath to Bergson's day, and it remains useful as an introduction to thinkers often known only by name.
52814-the-philosophy-of-giambattista-vic:
Philosophy of Giambattista Vico is a study by Benedetto Croce, rendered into English by R G Collingwood. Collingwood was a fellow of an Oxford college. The New York edition is dated nineteen thirteen. A translator's note says the book renders an Italian work of nineteen eleven. It also holds a paper of nineteen twelve, placed as an appendix. The whole translation was revised by the author, the note adds.

Contents run to nineteen chapters. Vico's theory of knowledge, in two phases, opens the set. The inner structure of his New Science follows. Imaginative knowledge in poetry and language, then myth and religion, take their turns. Morality, law, providence, and reflux fill the middle. Homer and primitive poetry and the history of Rome close the list.
53698-life-and-public-services-of-martin:
Life and Public Services of Martin Delany is a biography by Frank Rollin, printed at Boston in 1883. Delany served as sub-assistant commissioner of the bureau for refugees and freedmen. He was late a major of the 104th United States Colored Troops. Thirty-six chapters and an appendix fill the book.

Rollin follows Delany from genealogy and early schooling through his editorial career and medical practice. Canada, Captain John Brown, and the Harper's Ferry convention take their chapters. A council-chamber scene with President Lincoln stands near the heart. Later chapters place Delany at Charleston and Fort Sumter, and at work among freedmen. The appendix adds his political writings and African explorations.
56007-the-sagamore-of-saco:
Mrs E Oakes Smith tells a tale of early Maine in a dime novel issued by Beadle and Company in 1868. The story was number 142 in Beadle's Dime Novels, a semi-monthly series of cheap fiction. Its opening scene brings two colonial leaders together over wayward children.

Captain Richard Bonyton calls his son John a wild renegade and a shame to the colony. Sir Richard Vines answers more gently, noting that breaking from old society sows wildness in the young. Talk turns to Vines's daughter, and the two men clasp hands over a shared grief. Readers get frontier romance in the dime novel manner, with love, honor, and settlement life on the Saco in the first English years.
57223-airplane-boys-discover-the-secrets:
E J Craine's Airplane Boys Discover the Secrets of Cuzco was copyrighted in 1930 by the World Syndicate Publishing Company of Cleveland and New York. A note calls it the third book about the Airplane Boys: they get a marvelous new plane, which they name the Lark, and which serves them in many a narrow escape.

The contents run from Afire and Tracks in the Snow through Pigeon Jute, In the Lab, Out of the Sky, and Parts Unknown, to At Cuzco and Amy-Ran Fastness. The first chapter opens with Bob Caldwell riding toward a ranch. He shivers at the memory of taking Sergeant Bradshaw and Allen Ruhel, of the Canadian Royal Mounties, to identify the outlaws. The Gordons, senior and junior, have been forced to vacate, and the old man is safely in prison.
57335-light-and-colour-theories-and-thei:
Joseph Lovibond sets out his system in Light and Colour Theories and their Relation to Light and Colour Standardization, published by Spon in London and New York in 1915. Eleven plates, coloured by hand, include medals won by his method of colour analysis. An errata slip corrects a misplaced indigo line in the Newton plate.

Lovibond states his purpose plainly: colour is a determinable property of matter, and his methods of analysis have set standards of purity in some industries. Chapters run from the evolution of his unit through colour scales, charts, and figures in three dimensions. Appendices take up colour education, a standard light unit, and a radiometer. Plates even compare curves of healthy and diseased blood by his tintometer.
57900-lighthouses-and-lightships-a-descr:
Lighthouses and Lightships is a descriptive and historical account of their construction and organization by W H Davenport Adams, printed at New York in 1870. It belongs to the Illustrated Library of Wonders, with sixty illustrations. A plate shows the Eddystone Lighthouse. Adams also wrote Buried Cities of Campania and Queen of the Adriatic.

He opens by granting that every Englishman appreciates the lighthouse system that protects seamen against the dangers of the British shores. But it may reasonably be doubted, he says, whether the general public has any correct idea of its completeness. Few know the principles of its management, or the steps by which it grew. The book sets out to supply that knowledge. It explains how the great sea lights are built on rocks and shoals, and how the lightships ride at their stations. Adams writes the engineering romance of the lights that guard the coast.
58943-the-past-and-the-present-condition:
A discourse by Henry Highland Garnet, delivered at Troy, New York, in 1848. The Female Benevolent Society of Troy heard it at their fifteenth anniversary. They asked for its publication, and Garnet consented. The pamphlet prints their request and his reply. His theme is the past and present condition and the destiny of the coloured race.

Garnet invites his hearers to a high vantage point. The present stands midway between past and future. Behind lies an empire of ruin, dim through the mists of ages. Ahead, bright scenery promises truth, love, and liberty descending. Garnet had escaped slavery in Maryland as a child. He became a Presbyterian minister and a leading abolitionist voice. This early address shows his prophetic, oratorical style in full force.
59490-girl-scouts-in-arizona-and-new-mex:
Girl Scouts in Arizona and New Mexico is a girls adventure tale by Lillian Roy. Grosset and Dunlap of New York issued the book, with rights in nineteen twenty three. Roy also wrote the Polly Brewster books and the Little Washingtons books. Chapters follow scout plans for a trip to the Southwest lands.

The troop rides the old Santa Fe trail and camps in Pecos forests. Lost burros, a forest ranger turn, and rustlers stir the middle chapters. Ancient ruins, Padre Miguel story, and the Enchanted Mesa add local colour. Saint Michael Mission, the Painted Desert, and petrified forests come near the close. The Bright Angel Trail forms the last chapter of the trip.
59791-the-writing-of-news-a-handbook-wit:
Charles Ross, assistant professor of journalism at the University of Missouri, wrote The Writing of News as a handbook for reporters and copy readers. Henry Holt published it at New York in November 1911.

Early chapters cover preparing copy, the English of the newspapers, and the writer's viewpoint: fairness, impersonality, good taste, and originality. Accuracy in names, addresses, and spelling gets its own chapter. The lead and the story proper follow, with a study of 100 typical stories. Later chapters treat the feature story, the interview, the correspondent, copy reading, and writing the head. Closing chapters list the don'ts for news writers and collect the bromides of the trade.
6076-the-legends-of-san-francisco:
George W. Caldwell celebrates San Francisco on her seven hills, smiling beside an opalescent sunset sea. Bracing air, tingling sea breeze, and rolling fog drive heat languors out and thrill loyal subjects with joy of living. When summer heat oppresses the valleys, the city on the bay stays cool.

Caldwell promises the Indian's reasons for the city's charms and lures, never told before, in legends of hills, fog, and redwood bowers. Winter rains and sun lay a multicolored carpet of flowers on the land. The book gathers local legend into verse and prose, honoring a city of fog, hills, and restless energy.
6205-when-valmond-came-to-pontiac-the-st:
Parker's complete When Valmond Came to Pontiac repeats the introduction of a book standing by itself, an historical fantasy following The Trail of the Sword and preceding The Seats of the Mighty. Appearing in summer 1895, it won gratifying critics, one journal calling it written at a sitting, another a tour de force.

The grave Athenaeum praised it in a key that might make Parker nervous, setting a hard standard to preserve. In truth, Parker says, the book was written, printed, revised, and ready for press in five weeks, its manuscript complete within four. This complete edition is described from its introduction, gathering the lost Napoleon tale.
62423-history-of-madeley-including-ironb:
John Randall compiles the History of Madeley, Including Ironbridge, Coalbrookdale, and Coalport, published at the Wrekin Echo Office in Madeley in 1880. The title page promises notices of remarkable events, inventions, and phenomena, and manufactures, with twelve wood-cut illustrations and photographs, a copious index, and a list of old family names. Randall had written The Severn Valley and a history of Broseley.

His preface aims to lay before the people of Madeley the phases of its progress from feudal times to the present. Norman tillers, swineherds, fishermen, and the monks of Wenlock Priory open the tale; the Brooke family follows.
62449-maximilian-in-mexico:
Maximilian in Mexico, one of the Life Stories for Young People, was translated from the German of Kemper by George Upton and published by McClurg and Company at Chicago in 1911. Upton's preface calls the tale one of the saddest of tragedies. Maximilian, an Austrian archduke, was pressed to take the Mexican throne on the promise that the people had chosen him.

Louis Napoleon, who had sent him, broke his agreements, withdrew the French troops, and left him to his enemies. The Empress Carlotta, who had crossed to Europe to plead for help, sank into madness in an asylum. The chapters run from the emperor's arrival and first measures through church affairs and the siege of Querétaro to his capture and death with his generals. Upton says he died like a gentleman and a hero.
63233-china-s-revolution-1911-1912-a-his:
China's Revolution, 1911-1912 is Edwin Dingle's historical and political record of the Chinese civil war. McBride, Nast published it in New York in 1912, with two maps and thirty-six illustrations. A portrait of General Li Yuan Hung, the leader of the revolution, fronts the book. Dingle dedicates it to those who laid down their lives and to the New China party.

His note calls the book a popular history of the revolution that broke out at Wuchang in October 1911. Dingle was living at Hankow when the rising came, and he stayed through the war. He writes that the size of the revolution cannot yet be understood. His record served western readers as a first account of the fall of the Manchu dynasty.
63433-the-harvest-of-the-sea-a-contribut:
Harvest of the Sea treats the natural and trade history of British food fishes. James Bertram wrote the book for John Murray of London in eighteen sixty five. Fifty illustrations picture the fisheries, from Wick harbour herring season on. A Hamlet fishmonger jest stands as motto on the title page.

Bertram thanks French officials and Professor Coste of the French Institute for aid. Help also came from Huningue and the Paris acclimatisation garden staff. Polperro naturalist Jonathan Couch and sundry Scots informants gave facts too. The book surveys herring, and other food fish wealth of British seas. Fishermen, curers, and merchants all figure in its economic account.
63912-the-american-encyclopedia-of-histo:
The American Encyclopedia of History, Biography and Travel, by Thomas H Prescott, was published at Columbus by J & H Miller in 1857 and sold exclusively by subscription. The title page promises ancient and modern history, the biography of eminent men of Europe and America, and the lives of distinguished travelers.

Over one hundred engravings illustrate the volume, beginning with Washington's house at Mount Vernon. Prescott's preface argues that students of history should start with a compendium giving a general view of the whole subject. His historical department covers China, India, Egypt, and Arabia, then Syria, the Jews, Assyria, and Babylon. It runs through Greece and Rome, the dark ages, and the leading nations of modern Europe and the United States.
65654-brave-british-soldiers-and-the-vic:
S O Beeton edited a boys' volume on brave British soldiers and the Victoria Cross for his Boy's Own Library. A picture shows Corporal Robert Shields of the Royal Welsh Fusiliers finding his wounded adjutant's body. The title promises a general account of the regiments and men of the British army. Stories tell the brave deeds that won the prize for valour.

Sixteen full page engravings illustrate the text. Ward, Lock and Tyler published it at Paternoster Row. The series bound volumes handsomely at five shillings, or six with gilt edges. Beeton's library put military heroism before boy readers as a model of duty and courage.
65873-art-and-pleasure-painting-with-nee:
Book 54 of the Virginia Snow Studios of Elgin, Illinois, sold for ten cents as a crochet pattern book. Virginia Snow signs the introduction. The Romans, she says, called all fine sewing painting with needles, and millions of American women now paint so in colorful yarns. The book's business is to sell Dexter Cotton Warp, and to teach new uses for it.

Snow promises patterns from all over the world: designs first conceived by Colonial grandames, Spanish women, and Bavarian peasants, with instructions simple and easy to follow. A history of the Dexter mills follows the pitch. For a hundred and twenty years, the book says, American women have used Dexter cottons, since the founder dreamed his magic in rugged New England. The booklet is part pattern collection, part advertisement, and wholly of its mail-order moment.
65891-el-morro-trails-el-morro-national-:
El Morro Trails is a guide booklet for El Morro National Monument in New Mexico. It sold for fifty cents to visitors who took it home. The booklet walks the Inscription Rock Trail, which starts behind the monument headquarters. The climb is gentle, but the 7,200 feet of altitude may trouble some walkers, it warns.

The walk past the inscriptions and back takes thirty to forty minutes. Walkers may climb over the rock to two large prehistoric Indian ruins, adding an hour or more. Numbered stations on the path match numbered paragraphs in the booklet. It also warns of rattlesnakes and asks visitors to leave the place neat. The guide explains the names carved in the rock by travellers of past centuries.
66265-a-general-history-of-the-sabbatari:
A General History of the Sabbatarian Churches, by Mrs Tamar Davis, traces the communities that kept the seventh day as Sabbath across Asia, Africa, Europe, and America. Lindsay and Blakiston of Philadelphia published the book in 1851. Davis wrote while the Sabbath controversy filled conventions and unions across the country, and she offers no apology for adding her work to the argument.

Her accounts embrace the Armenian, East Indian, and Abyssinian churches, then the Waldenses, Semi-Judaisers, and Sabbatarian Anabaptists of Europe. The Seventh-day Baptist denomination in the United States closes the survey. Her side contends that the Sabbath was changed not by Christ or his apostles but by church synods and councils. Churches too distant to feel that authority, she holds, prove the point by their practice.
66484-the-doctrines-and-discipline-of-th:
The Doctrines and Discipline of the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church is dated 1918. The church's own agent and publishers copyrighted this revised edition. Its text runs to fifty eight chapters in nine parts. The ninth part holds the ritual of the church. An episcopal address opens the book. The bishops commend the discipline to every member's house. Read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest the whole, they urge. The articles of religion stand inside, they note. No member should be ignorant of his church's doctrine, they write. A short history of the connection follows the address. The church had always been part of the Methodist family, it says.

First it stood within the Methodist Episcopal Church in America. The division of 1844 placed it in the southern branch. From that branch its own organisation was formed.
66521-the-passing-of-morocco:
Frederick Moore wrote The Passing of Morocco, a war reporter’s book on the fall of old Morocco. Houghton, Mifflin, and Company issued it in Boston and New York in nineteen hundred eight. Moore had written The Balkan Trail before this. Maps and photos run through the tale of camps and coasts.

Moore landed at Gibraltar in August nineteen hundred seven off a steamer. British soldiers and police ruled that Rock in plain sight. Moors crossed the town as guests in a land not theirs. French columns and the Foreign Legion fill his war chapters. No quarter, forced marches, and holy war mark the hard road. Tangier, Rabat, and pirate Salli show the coast in turn. Raisuli, safe under British guard, earns a chapter of note. Sultans rise and crowd as the old realm fades out.
67027-turquois-mosaic-art-in-ancient-mex:
Marshall Saville studies turquois mosaic art in ancient Mexico for the Museum of the American Indian, Heye Foundation, in 1922. The book forms volume six of the museum's contributions series, printed in New York. Saville dedicates it to George Gustav Heye, whose interest built the museum.

Early chapters gather the first written accounts, from the Grijalva expedition of 1518 and loot taken by Cortés from 1519 to 1525. Tribute paid to Aztec rulers, sources of turquois, and the work of Aztec stone workers follow. The main catalogue then describes surviving pieces: masks, skull masks, shields, helmets, knife handles, and animal figures held in museums from London to New York.
68519-the-urine-dance-of-the-zuni-indian:
Captain John Bourke of the Third Cavalry wrote The Urine Dance of the Zuni Indians of New Mexico, privately printed in 1920 from ethnological notes collected in 1881 under Sheridan's direction. The pamphlet is marked not for general perusal. On the evening of November 17, 1881, the Nehue-Cue secret order sent word they would honour Bourke and Cushing with a dance.

Squaws of the governor's family swept the long living room and sprinkled water to lay the dust for the visit. Twelve dancers entered after dark, two of them boys, the centre men naked save black breech-clouts of archaic style. Turkey feathers, corn-husk ear ornaments, white body paint, and tortoise rattles dressed them. Ethnology readers get a rare record.
68556-land-without-chimneys-or-the-byway:
Alfred Oscar Coffin wrote Land Without Chimneys, or the Byways of Mexico, issued at Cincinnati by the Editor Publishing Company in eighteen ninety eight. Coffin, a doctor of philosophy, gave the book to Professor Helen C Morgan, his former teacher. Twenty five chapters fill the travel book. Chapter one is The San Juan Valley. This book is not sent forth to fill a long felt want, he opens.

Nor does the author hope to convince all readers to his way of looking at the social and religious problems of Mexico, the preface grants. Saltillo and the Plateau, San Luis Potosi, and The Bill of Fare follow. In the Valley of the Laja and The Valley of Mexico fill the middle. The Shrine of Guadalupe, public buildings, and the Paseo and bull fight follow. Travel readers get a Black American scholar tour of Porfirian Mexico.
68938-a-campaign-in-mexico:
Scribner, a volunteer soldier, wrote this plain account of a campaign in Mexico. Gihon printed the book in Philadelphia in 1850. A plate of the Battle of Buena Vista fronts the volume. The author signs himself one who was there in the war.

His preface says pages were written in camp amid noise and want. He claims no literary merit, only a faithful, plain relation. Feelings, duties, fatigues, and perils of a volunteer fill the book. A Buena Vista map by Lieutenant Green backs the battle account. Officers praised the map as the truest yet made of that hard field.
69203-sketchbook-of-the-philadelphia-bos:
The Philadelphia and Boston Face Brick Company issued this sketch book from 165 Milk Street, Boston, entered for copyright in 1904. A preface to the seventeenth edition sings the fireplace. From time immemorial, it says, the domestic hearth has been the theme of optimists and poets. The fireplace is the happiest rallying-place of the family, the sun in the house. In recent years the chimney-piece has been made the central part of the decorative scheme of a room.

To all home-builders, the preface goes on, comes the thought that they must have at least one or two open fireplaces. As to materials for the mantel, nothing meets all needs so completely as the company's ornamental unglazed brick. A brick facing with a wooden mantel is a makeshift now passing by, the company argues, and its own brick mantels are patterned after Greek and Renaissance designs.
69519-new-system-of-domestic-cookery-for:
A New System of Domestic Cookery, formed on rules of thrift and made for private families, was issued in Boston in 1807 by a lady who gives no name. The author says the receipts were first meant for her own daughters, to help them set a good table without waste or show. She shuns rich extras and large use of meat for gravy.

Plain receipts cover daily foods that are often done badly, such as melted butter, toast and water, and coffee. The author makes no claim to write for trained cooks and asks for no profit from the book. Her aim is close, clear help for a young housekeeper who must feed a family well on a tight purse.
69783-a-synopsis-of-the-palms-of-puerto-:
Cook's synopsis of the palms of Puerto Rico, reprinted from the Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club for October 1901, offers provisional names for a hard group. The notes grew out of economic studies of the island's palms, and plates 43 to 48 accompany them.

Cook calls the palms a refractory group: hard to gather, hard to study dried, and neglected in field and herbarium alike. Old descriptions, he says, often fail to fix a species, and generic names have been loosely applied. The fibers of the leaf-bases give good marks, though no other plant family offers a parallel for them. A palm's narrow home range, he argues, can name it better than much printed description.
70601-archeology-of-the-lower-mimbres-va:
Archeology of the Lower Mimbres Valley, New Mexico is a report by Fewkes, issued by the Smithsonian Institution in 1914. It forms number ten of volume 63 of the Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections. Eight plates show the finds.

Fewkes opens with the short written record of the valley. Bartlett's Personal Narrative of 1854 is one of the first English accounts. Bartlett saw deer, turkeys, bears, and fine trout on his way to the copper mines at Santa Rita. He passed mounds that mark old ruins and said little of them. A party from his camp found broken pottery of fine make, painted in red, black, and brown. A stone mortar lay with it. Fewkes sets such traces in order and reads the valley's old Indian life from them.
74308-a-diplomat-s-wife-in-mexico:
Diplomat Wife in Mexico is a letter book by Edith O Shaughnessy. Harper of New York and London issued it in June nineteen sixteen. The letters come from the American Embassy at Mexico City in revolution days. They cover October eighth nineteen thirteen to April twenty third nineteen fourteen.

That end date marks the breaking off of relations between the two lands. An account of the occupation of Vera Cruz is added to the letters. Contents open with arrival at Vera Cruz and visits to the battleships. Huerta second coup, election day surprises, and embassy receptions follow in order. Feast of the Dead booths at the Alameda colour the social chapters.
75469-trading-with-mexico:
Wallace Thompson, author of 'The People of Mexico,' wrote this guide to American trade with Mexico, published in New York in 1921. He begins with three basic facts that, he says, fix the terms of that trade. Wet trips, warm feeling and loose promises, in his view, will not change those facts.

Chapters move from the Mexican market and its buyers to credit, debts left by revolution, oil and Yucatan. Thompson treats Mexico's land, people and politics as the ground any trader must know. The final chapter seeks a highway to a lasting fix for trade between the two countries.
77230-family-names-from-the-irish-anglo-:
Family Names from the Irish, Anglo-Saxon, Anglo-Norman, and Scotch, by Thomas Gentry, was published in Philadelphia in 1892. Gentry was known for life histories of birds of eastern Pennsylvania and a book on the house sparrow. Here he turns to word roots, asking what family names mean and where they came from.

His preface says that in all ages names have marked a person's traits, face, faith, place, or fate. Hebrew names such as Adam, for red earth, and Greek names have been well studied, he notes, while Latin and German names hold more doubt. Scholars such as Turner, Kemble, and Thierry worked on Saxon names but not side by side. Gentry aims to fill that gap for common readers.
78046-joan-and-co:
Joan and Company is a novel by Frederick Orin Bartlett, printed in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin under a 1919 copyright. Bartlett had written One Year of Pierrot, the Triflers, the Wall Street Girl, and Joan of the Alley. He gives the book to R S B.

Chapters open with Dicky is serious, Joan is bored, and chance. The driver and fate, bandaged, and whose fault follow. A letter, Dicky calls, and the fighting things pace the mid tale. At home, the silent partner, and Joan and Company come next. A challenge, pumpkin pie, and like Napoleon raise the stakes. The text shows Joan quizzical smile in dark eyes above a dainty nose. Her air of amused boredom first fascinated Dicky Burnett. Romance fans get a business and love tale of 1919.
78158-measles-diphtheria-scarlet-fever-c:
George Weaver, a Chicago professor of pathology, wrote this health guide as Little Blue Book number 136, copyrighted in 1924. Weaver ran the Durand Hospital of an institute for infectious diseases. The booklet belongs to a health series overseen by Morris Fishbein of the American Medical Association's journal staff.

Sections treat measles, diphtheria, scarlet fever, chicken pox, and whooping cough in turn. Each covers cause, spread, symptoms, complications, prevention, and treatment in plain order. Diphtheria also gets serum risks and a plan to wipe out its dangers. Readers get the cheap, pocket-sized medical advice that reached small towns by mail in the 1920s.
78600-carranza-and-mexico:
Carlo De Fornaro wrote this account of the Mexican Revolution for American readers, and Mitchell Kennerley published it at New York in 1915. Its center is Venustiano Carranza, First Chief of the Constitutionalists, who overthrew the Huerta dictatorship after eighteen months of victories. Chapters trace the Diaz regime, the Madero revolution and its fall, the plotting against Madero, and the landing of American Marines at Vera Cruz.

Other hands contribute chapters: a colonel of the revolution writes on the campaign in the west, and further pieces cover the money and the diplomacy of the cause. Villa in the north, Zapata in the south, and Obregon in the west get their own chapters, and the land question runs through the book. It is a partisan history, dedicated to President Woodrow Wilson.
79275-mexico:
George Barrie and Sons of Philadelphia published Mexico, a History of its Progress and Development in One Hundred Years, in 1911. Marie Robinson Wright, a member of geographical societies on three continents, wrote it. Porfirio Díaz, president of the republic, illustrates the front, and the dedication goes to him.

The book honors Díaz on his eightieth birthday: a great man among the eminent men of the world, still active in body and soul, a powerful administrator of his country's good. The hundred years run from the independence cry of 1810 to the centenary celebrations of 1910. Wright's Mexico is the regime's showroom: railways, mines, order, and progress, arranged for capital. Within months of publication the revolution had begun and Díaz was in exile. The centenary volume survives as the porcelain facade of a fallen order, printed before the cracking.
79691-shorty-goes-loco:
Shorty Goes Loco is a western story by Ray Humphreys. Deputy Sheriff Shorty McKay begs his boss for a case. Sheriff Joe Cook had held a conference in his office. Shorty sat through it with his nose in a book. The book, he protests, is no story book. Its title is Detective Disguises.

Shorty heard every word while pretending to read. He wants the trip to Alamosa, and maybe on to Salida or Pueblo. The sheriff dislikes the journey in such weather and weakens. He throws the disguise book into the waste basket. Then he gives the case, with warnings. Their suspicions are not yet sure, and Shorty must verify them before making a rumpus. The nine fifteen train sets the deadline. Humphreys tells the tale in heavy dialect, with Shorty as a comic mix of ambition, laziness, and nerve.
9364-life-in-mexico:
Frances Calderon de la Barca, born in Edinburgh in 1804, wrote this account of two years in Mexico. Daughter of William Inglis, she married the Spanish diplomat Don Angel Calderon de la Barca and followed his posts to Mexico, Washington, and Madrid. Alfonso the Twelfth later made her Marquesa, and she died in 1882.

With a preface by W. H. Prescott, her letters describe Mexican society, politics, and daily life with wit and keen eyes. She stands between worlds, Scots, Spanish, and Mexican at once. The book remains a classic of travel writing, vivid and humane.
a-counter-blaste-to-tobacco: King James the First blasts tobacco in this famous tract, first printed in 1604. Addressing his countrymen, he argues that even a healthy body is subject to disease, and tobacco adds harm rather than health. Edmund Goldsmid edited this later reprint for private circulation. The Counter-Blaste remains a landmark of early anti tobacco writing.
an-elegy-wrote-in-a-country-church-yard-: Thomas Gray writes his elegy in a country churchyard, presented here with the Eton College manuscript and a note on the texts. The poem meditates on humble lives, death, and unmarked graves, in verses that became among the best known in English. This edition lets readers compare the printed poem with its manuscript form.
animal-sanctuaries-in-labrador-an-addres: William Wood, lieutenant-colonel, presents an address on animal sanctuaries in Labrador before the second annual meeting of the Commission of Conservation at Quebec in January 1911. Printed in Ottawa, the address argues for protecting Labrador's wildlife in reserves. Wood's plea marks an early Canadian step toward conservation. His case still reads as plain common sense.
at-war-with-pontiac-or-the-totem-of-the-:
Kirk Munroe wrote this frontier tale for Charles Scribner's Sons, copyrighted in 1895 and reprinted in 1922 with pictures by J. Finnemore. Munroe sets his story in Pontiac's War, when Ottawa chief Pontiac rose against the British after the French and Indian War. Young Donald and Major Hester carry the action between forts, camps, and wilderness trails.

Chapters promise escapes of prisoners, a baby lost and recovered, and Donald sent on a perilous mission. Pontiac declares war, the major is taken prisoner, and a white medicine man and the totem of the bear shape later turns. Canoe pursuits across a lake, with pursuers yelling once discovered, show Munroe's pace: history delivered as breathless boys' adventure in the Redcoat-and-Redskin manner.
berry-and-co:
Dornford Yates published this set of linked comic tales with Ward, Lock, introducing Berry Pleydell and his circle in book form. A prefatory letter to Valerie confesses the author's dangerous affection for passages in the book. Berry, his wife Daphne, and the faithful Jonah and Boy move between London and the country house White Ladies, where the whole party summers in state.

Domestic logistics supply the war. The household faces leaving town in a month, wholly at the mercy of whoever controls the kitchen at White Ladies. With no restaurants or clubs to fall back on, a bad cook means an unpalatable season. Yates writes upper-class farce in mandarin prose: motor cars, stolen marches, and misunderstandings, all polished until the silliness gleams like good silver.
biographical-memorials-of-james-oglethor:
Thaddeus Mason Harris published these memorials of James Oglethorpe in 1841, dedicating the work to the Georgia Historical Society. Harris, a Massachusetts clergyman and antiquary, honours the founder of the colony of Georgia with a full life. Oglethorpe's example, the dedication verse promises, will shine as a favourite theme with poet and divine, and posterity shall add new honours to his name.

Campaigning in the Georgia backcountry fills the sampled pages. Oglethorpe's party forced through tangled thickets and deep, broken ravines, crossed swamps where horses mired and plunged, and rafted great rivers while the horses swam. Their resolute leader slept in the open air wrapped in his cloak, a portmanteau for his pillow. Harris writes the philanthropic general — prison reformer, coloniser, and soldier — for a young state learning to revere its founder.
britannica-1911-acapulco:
Acapulco is a city and port of the state of Guerrero on Mexico's Pacific coast, south-west of Mexico City, with about five thousand people at the 1900 census. Its deep, semicircular bay is almost land-locked, easy to enter, and so secure that vessels can lie alongside the rocks. The entry calls it the best harbour on Mexico's Pacific coast and a port of call between Panama and San Francisco.

Mountains crowd the town onto a narrow strip of low land and make its climate exceptionally hot and unhealthy. For centuries Acapulco was Mexico's chief Pacific port and the depot for Spanish fleets trading with the East Indies, a trade lost at independence. Hides, cedar, and fruit head its exports.
britannica-1911-alberti-domenico:
Domenico Alberti (about 1710–1740), an Italian player and composer, left his name on a pattern every piano pupil meets: the Alberti bass. He wrote dozens of sonatas on one plan. The tune rides on top from first bar to last, while the bass hand breaks chords into arpeggio runs beneath it. The device grew so common that players tagged it with his name.

His sonatas also mark a shift in taste. The feel for polyphony, the weaving of free voices each with its own line, had worn thin even in Bach's own days, and Alberti's work shows the loss. The pieces hold no other marked traits, the verdict runs. Yet they reached ahead in time. Mozart's first violin sonatas, penned at the age of seven, were most likely built on Alberti's model, though the boy's work outshone it in cleverness.
britannica-1911-alfani-domenico:
Friendship with Raphael shaped the art of Domenico Alfani, a painter born at Perugia near the end of the fifteenth century. Both men trained under Perugino, and they stayed close. Raphael's mark on Alfani's pictures runs so deep that buyers and critics have often handed those pictures to Raphael himself.

Late in life Alfani drifted from his Perugian training toward the newer Florentine manner. Even his death stays unsettled: one account gives 1540, while another has him living in 1553. His works hang at Florence and in a number of churches in Perugia, the city of his birth.
britannica-1911-arauco:
Arauco is a coast province of southern Chile. Concepción bounds it on the north. Bio-bio, Malleco, and Cautin surround it otherwise. Its area is 2,458 square miles. Population was estimated at 70,635 in 1902. The province covered independent Araucania once. That Indian territory was later divided. Four provinces emerged from the division. Arauco was one of them.

Agriculture dominates the province's pursuits. Lebú is its capital town. Lebú stands on the coast. Concepción lies fifty-five miles north of it. A railway connects the two towns. Lebú's population was 3,178 in 1902. The entry is a brief gazetteer notice. It complements the Araucania article directly. Together they map Chile's southern frontier provinces.
britannica-1911-ariosto-lodovico:
Lodovico Ariosto, an Italian poet who lived from 1474 to 1533, is profiled at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Reggio, he loved poetry from youth but was forced by his father to study law. He lost five years to that study. When freed, he turned to Latin classics under a skilled teacher.

His father died soon after, and Ariosto had to run a large family in hard straits. He cared for nine brothers and sisters on a tight income. Still, he wrote plays in prose and lyric verse that drew notice. Cardinal Ippolito d Este took him into his household as a patron. The entry is sharp on that bond. The cardinal paid poorly, paid late, and used the poet as a messenger at risk to his life.
britannica-1911-barbieri-giovanni-france:
Giovanni Francesco Barbieri (1591-1666), called Guercino from his squint, was an Italian painter, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces his rapid rise. He was born at Cento, a village near Bologna, and his powers grew so fast that at seventeen he was working with a known painter of the Bolognese school. His fame spread beyond his village, and in 1615 he moved to Bologna, where his paintings were much admired.

His first style followed the Caracci, but the strong colour and shadow of Caravaggio struck him deeply and marked his work for a long stretch. Some late pieces lean toward the lighter, clearer manner of his great contemporary Guido. Guercino stood in the first rank for his fellow artists and for the nobles and princes of Italy. He was famed for speed, finishing no fewer than 106 large altar-pieces, the entry begins to count.
britannica-1911-bartolozzi-francesco:
Francesco Bartolozzi (1725–1815), an Italian engraver born at Florence, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. His father was a gold- and silver-smith, and the son was at first meant for that trade. Skill in drawing changed the plan. Florentine artists taught him painting for three years before he went to Venice to study engraving. There he advanced fast and produced work of real importance while still young.

London became Bartolozzi's base for nearly forty years from 1764. There he turned out an enormous number of engravings, many after Cipriani and Angelica Kauffmann, and contributed plates to Boydell's Shakespeare Gallery. His Clytie after Annibale Caracci and Virgin and Child after Carlo Dolce are picked out as his best. In 1802 he moved to Lisbon as director of the National Academy and stayed in Portugal until his death. His son Gaetano was also an engraver.
britannica-1911-berni-francesco:
Francesco Berni (1497–1536) was an Italian poet born at Lamporecchio, near the upper Arno. His family was well descended but very poor. He went to Florence, then to Rome at nineteen. There he served as secretary to Ghiberti, datary to Clement VII. The desk work irked him greatly. Yet Rome made him famous for wit.

The 1911 Britannica entry places Berni at the head of Italian burlesque poets. Mocking comic verse is still called poesie bernesca after him. About 1530 he gained a canonry at Florence cathedral. He died there in 1536, by tradition poisoned by Duke Alessandro. His reworking of Boiardo's Orlando, the Rifacimento, appeared after his death in 1541.
britannica-1911-bianchini-francesco:
Francesco Bianchini, an Italian astronomer and antiquary who lived from 1662 to 1729, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born of a noble family at Verona, he went to Rome in 1684. He became librarian to a cardinal who, as pope, raised him to high offices. A later pope sent him on a mission to Paris in 1712 and set him to form a museum.

That museum was to hold Christian antiquities, the entry says. Bianchini died at Rome in March 1729. His writings listed here include a universal history, of which only one volume appeared. He also wrote on the calendar and on the planet Venus. In that work he claimed Venus turns once in a span of many days. Later editors issued his chosen observations and his smaller works after his death.
britannica-1911-botzaris-marco:
Marco Botzaris (about 1788–1823) was a Suliot leader in the Greek war of independence, still sung in Greek ballads. Born at Suli in Albania, second son of Kitzo Botzaris, he fled to the Ionian Islands when Ali Pasha took Suli in 1803. There he served in an Albanian regiment in French pay.

He joined the secret patriotic society, the Hetairia Philike, in 1814, and in 1820 made common cause with Ali of Iannina against the Ottomans. When revolt broke he won fame as a partisan leader in western Greece and stood out in the first defence of Missolonghi in 1822–1823. On the night of 21 August 1823 he led 350 Suliots against 4000 Albanians at Karpenisi and routed them, but fell in the fight. His brother Kosta finished the victory.
britannica-1911-bronco: Bronco is a Spanish word meaning rough or rude, applied to an unbroken or untamed horse, in the United States especially a mustang. The whole hosted entry is that single-sentence definition. It gives the word's Spanish root and sense, fixes its American use for a wild or half-wild horse, notes that the word entered America by way of Mexico. The entry warns that the spelling Broncho, though common, is incorrect.
britannica-1911-caracciolo-francesco:
Francesco Caracciolo (1732–1799) was a Neapolitan admiral and revolutionist. He was a prince of a noble Naples family. This 1911 Britannica entry tells his tragic story. He was born on 18 January 1732. He entered the navy young and learned seamanship under Rodney. He fought with distinction in British service. His wars included the American War of Independence. He also fought Barbary pirates and the French at Toulon.

The Bourbon court trusted Caracciolo above all Neapolitans. In December 1798 the king and queen fled Naples. They fled to Sicily on Nelson's ship Vanguard. Caracciolo escorted them on the frigate Sannita. Even his loyalty was shaken by the king's cowardly flight. At Palermo he asked leave to return to Naples. The city was drunk on French revolutionary ideas. The aristocracy and middle classes welcomed him with enthusiasm. He was pressed to join the new republic or flee.
britannica-1911-cariaco:
Cariaco is a town on the north coast of Venezuela. It is also called San Felipe de Austria. It stands 40 miles east of the city of Cumaná. It sits at the head of the gulf of the same name. Its population was estimated at 7000 in 1908. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives its trade. The town stands a short way up the Cariaco river.

Its port, right on the coast, is called Puerto Sucre. The district around Cariaco grows several cash crops. Cotton, tobacco and cacao are its named products. Cattle and fruit also come from the district. Trade through Puerto Sucre is considerable, the entry says. Yet that port has no regular link with foreign ports. The whole notice is a brief paragraph in the original. It gives the site, the port and the farm produce.
britannica-1911-cavalli-francesco:
Francesco Cavalli (1599?–1676) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian composer born at Crema. His real name was Pier Francesco Caletti-Bruni. Cavalli was the name of his patron, a Venetian nobleman. He became a singer at St Mark's in Venice in 1617. He rose to second organist in 1639, first organist in 1665, and maestro di cappella in 1668.

His fame, though, rests on his operas. He began writing for the stage in 1639. Paris summoned him in 1660 to produce Serse at the Louvre for the marriage of Louis XIV. He returned in 1662 with Ercole Amante. Twenty seven of his operas survive, most of them at St Mark's library in Venice. The entry credits him with making opera a popular entertainment. He trimmed Monteverde's large orchestra, added tuneful arias, and used popular types in his libretti.
britannica-1911-cirillo-domenico:
Domenico Cirillo was an Italian healer and friend of freedom who lived from seventeen thirty-nine to seventeen ninety-nine. He was born at Grumo in the realm of Naples. While young he took a chair in plant lore, then went to England and France. He was made a peer of the chief science group in London.

Back in Naples he held chairs in the heal art and built a wide work with the sick. When French hosts set up a new free state, he took a seat in its law group and rose to lead it. The old king came back, a truce was broke, and he was put to death.
britannica-1911-comparetti-domenico:
Domenico Comparetti was an Italian scholar who was born at Rome in eighteen thirty-five. He took a degree in science and sums, then worked in the shop of his uncle. His free hours went to books, and he taught himself Greek by talk with Greek youths at his school. That hard path made him a chief Greek scholar of Italy.

A chair of Greek at Pisa came in eighteen fifty-nine, then one at Florence. His books run from old Greek speech to the great song tale of Finland. He held that a vast epic can not be sewn from folk songs. His work on Virgil is also famed.
britannica-1911-cordoba-mexico:
Cordoba, a town in the state of Vera Cruz, Mexico, is set out in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies west of the port of Vera Cruz, in a rich valley near the volcano Orizaba. The town stands close to three thousand feet above the sea.

The district round it grows sugar, tobacco, and coffee. Cordoba is one of the chief coffee centres of Mexico, the entry says. Cotton and wool cloth are also made there. The town is laid out in a regular plan and built of stone. Its old cathedral is the chief building named. Cordoba was a place of weight in colonial times. It fell away after the revolt, then gained back trade through rail and coffee.
britannica-1911-corisco:
Corisco, the name of a bay and an island on the Guinea Coast of West Africa, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The bay runs about thirty-one miles across and some fifteen miles inland. Sandbanks crowd it and cut its worth as a harbour. The Muni river flows in on its north side, deep in itself but reached by a shallow channel.

The bay holds many small isles, some drowned at high tide. The chief isles are Bana, Great and Little Elobey, and Corisco, the last farthest out to sea. Corisco island is about three miles long and holds hills and vales, woods and swamps, and lakes in small compass. Its woods yield ebony and logwood for export. The people are the Benga, and the isles are Spanish lands ruled from Fernando Po.
britannica-1911-correa-da-serra-jose-fra:
Jose Francisco Correa da Serra was a Portuguese leader and man of science born in the south of Portugal. Schooled at Rome, he took church orders under the wing of a great duke, kin to the queen. Back in Lisbon he lived with his patron and helped found the national school of sciences of Portugal.

The 1911 Britannica entry says he was made its life long clerk, with the rare right to print its works with no censor to check them. Use of that right set him at odds with the church court, and he fled to France. Home again, he gave a room in the palace to a French exile of the revolt, and had to flee once more, this time to England. There a great patron of science took him up.
britannica-1911-cosenz-enrico:
Enrico Cosenz lived from 1812 to 1898 and was an Italian soldier. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Gaeta, where he was born in January 1812. As a captain of artillery he marched against Austria in 1848. Naples had sent that force north under King Ferdinand the Second. When the king called the troops back, Cosenz refused the order in protest.

He went with General Pepe to help defend Venice in its revolt. At the fort of Marghera he showed great valour in command. Twice wounded, he held the Piazzale after that fort fell at last. When Venice fell he fled to Piedmont for safety and rest. In 1859 he took command of a Garibaldian regiment for new wars.
britannica-1911-crispi-francesco:
Francesco Crispi (1819–1901) was an Italian statesman born at Ribera in Sicily on 4 October 1819. He set up as an advocate at Naples in 1846. When revolution broke out at Palermo in January 1848 he hurried home and helped guide the rising. The Bourbon return in 1849 shut him out of the amnesty and drove him to Piedmont. There he lived poorly by journalism and plotted with Mazzini's circle.

Crispi helped organize Garibaldi's expedition of the Thousand in 1860 and drafted the proclamation at Salemi. He entered parliament in 1861 for Castelvetrano on the extreme Left. The later pages trace his rise to power and his firm foreign policy. He courted good relations with France yet refused to bend to pressure or dictation. Criticism of him, the entry says, fixed more on his private life and his circle than on his public acts.
britannica-1911-curico:
Curicó is a province of central Chile, and a gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its land and goods. The province lies between Colchagua and Talca. It runs from the Pacific coast to the Argentine frontier. Its area comes to 2,978 square miles, and its count to 103,242 in 1895.

The east and west sections of the province are mountain country. Between them lies the fertile valley of central Chile. Mineral wealth is present but little worked, the entry says. Copper, gold, and silver are all said to occur there. Cattle, wheat, and wine are the chief products of the province. Indian corn and fruit are grown as well. On the coast, salt making is a key industry. The climate is mild, with more rain than the north of the valley.
britannica-1911-cuzco:
Cuzco is an inland city of south Peru, seat of a high land department of the same name, far east of Lima. Its folk, most of them Indians and mixed blood, were set at a high count in one year and a much less count in the next count a decade on. The city stands at the head of a small vale at a vast height above the sea.

Hills of great size ring it near on all sides. The 1911 Britannica entry names the famed hill that looks down on the town from the north. On it stand the ruins of the vast stone fort of the Incas and of those who came before them. Two streams cut deep gullies at its sides. The main part of the city lies between those streams, with its great square at its heart.
britannica-1911-fieschi-giuseppe-marco:
Giuseppe Marco Fieschi, born in Corsica in seventeen ninety, led a famed attack on Louis Philippe. He had served under Murat, then returned to Corsica after the wars. There he was sentenced to ten years in jail for theft and forgery. Police were to watch him for life after his release. After a spell of wandering he got a small post in Paris by forged papers.

When Fieschi lost that post he vowed revenge on society as a whole. With two comrades he built a device of twenty gun barrels in his lodgings. All twenty barrels were set to fire at one moment as one blast. On the twenty eighth of July eighteen thirty five the king passed along the boulevard. The device was fired as the royal party rode past. The king was grazed, a marshal was killed, and many bystanders were hurt.
britannica-1911-filelfo-francesco:
Francesco Filelfo was an Italian scholar who lived from thirteen ninety-eight to fourteen eighty-one. He was born at Tolentino. By his youth the first great work to bring back old Roman books was done. He was to push that work on and help bring back Greek books as well.

The entry tells how he taught at Venice while still young and won fame at once. A post at the court in Constantinople let him learn Greek from a famed teacher there. He wed the daughter of that teacher and built a large store of Greek books. His later life was a round of posts, books, and feuds.
britannica-1911-fontana-domenico:
Domenico Fontana (1543-1607), Italian architect and mechanician, was born at Mili, a village on Lake Como, in 1543. After good training in mathematics he went in 1563 to join his elder brother, who was studying architecture at Rome. He advanced fast and entered the service of Cardinal Montalto. For him he built a chapel in Santa Maria Maggiore and the villa Negroni. When the pope stopped the cardinal's pension, Fontana offered to finish the works in hand at his own cost.

The cardinal was soon elected pope as Sixtus V, and he made Fontana his chief architect at once. The Lateran palace, the Quirinal palace and the Vatican library are among his works. His highest fame came from moving the great Egyptian obelisk that Caligula had brought to Rome. The entry tells how the huge stone was raised and set up, the engineering feat by which Fontana is still remembered.
britannica-1911-geminiani-francesco:
Francesco Geminiani (c. 1680–1762) was an Italian violinist, born at Lucca about 1680. He took music lessons from Alessandro Scarlatti. He studied the violin under Lunati, called Gobbo, and then under Corelli. In 1714 he came to London, where the earl of Essex took him under his care. He made his living there by teaching and by writing music. In 1715 he played his violin concertos with Handel at the English court.

After a stay in Paris, Geminiani came back to England in 1755. In 1761 he went to Dublin, where a servant stole a music draft on which he had spent much time and work. His grief at that loss is said to have hastened his death in 1762. The article calls him a first-rate player, but finds most of his works dry and short on tune.
britannica-1911-goya-y-lucientes-francis:
Francisco Goya y Lucientes, a Spanish painter, opens a bold art life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in seventeen forty six at a small Aragon town, he learned art with a local master. That master had learned his craft at Naples in Italy. Fine draw skill from that line did not tame the wild pupil. Brawls at church feasts mark his youth in the home town tales.

At age nineteen his friends sent him to Madrid to save his name. Song and night sport filled his days in the chief town then. No royal funds came his way for the Rome trip of art youths. He joined a band of bull fighters to earn his way to the sea. Rome took him in at last, sick and with no cash in hand.
britannica-1911-grazzini-antonio-frances:
Antonio Francesco Grazzini, an Italian author who lived from 1503 to 1583, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Florence to a good family, he seems to have worked early as an apothecary. In 1540 he helped found the Academy of the Humid. He later helped set up the famed Accademia della Crusca.

In both groups he was known by the name Il Lasca. His sharp tongue stirred many literary quarrels. His peers once cast him out for fierce attacks on a rival party. He was taken back in 1566 when a friend led the group. The entry ranks him as a master of Tuscan prose. His style is rich, supple, and full of the force of common speech. His chief works are a set of tales in the manner of Boccaccio and a run of prose comedies.
britannica-1911-guardi-francesco:
Francesco Guardi (1712–1793) was a Venetian painter. He was a pupil of Canaletto. He followed his master's style very closely. His pictures are often attributed to Canaletto himself. Yet the difference, once seen, is marked. Canaletto is firmer, solider and more distinct. Guardi shows a more spirited touch. His colour sparkles, and his figures are sketched with flair.

Guardi sometimes coloured Canaletto's own designs. His speed was extraordinary. Three or four days could produce an entire work. That facility, and a love of gain, made his output large. Many of his works are found in England. Seven hang in the Louvre. The entry is a compact judgement on a painter long standing in his master's shadow.
britannica-1911-guicciardini-francesco:
Francesco Guicciardini (1483–1540) was an Italian historian and statesman. He was born at Florence in 1483. His family had held Florence's highest posts for generations. Marsilio Ficino held him at his baptism. He studied at Ferrara and Padua until 1505. An uncle's death tempted him toward the church. His father forbade any son entering so corrupt a body.

Guicciardini turned instead to law. At twenty-three he lectured publicly on the Institutes. He married Maria Salviati for political support. He says so frankly in his own memoirs. In 1512 Florence sent him as ambassador to Ferdinand of Spain. His Spanish letters show extraordinary powers of observation. Critics accused him of betraying Florence for the Medici. A long career as diplomat and governor followed. His great history of Italy crowns the later account.
britannica-1911-herrera-francisco:
Francisco Herrera, called the Old, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in fifteen seventy six, he was a Spanish painter of history scenes and wall works. He studied under Luis Fernandez in Seville, his home city. He spent most of his life in that city.

The entry is frank about his rough ways, which drove pupils and children away. Yet his great skill brought him many commissions. He also worked well in bronze, a skill that led to a charge of making false coin. He took refuge in a Jesuit college and painted its patron saint. King Philip the Fourth saw that work and pardoned him.
britannica-1911-huanuco:
Huanuco is a city of central Peru, capital of a department of the same name, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes both. The city stands in a fine valley on the left bank of the Huallaga river, nearly 6,000 feet above the sea, with about 6,000 people. It was founded in 1539 by Gomez Alvarado.

The entry says the town is famed for its fruits and sweetmeats, its custard apples being the largest and best of their kind, and that mining is one of its trades. It also recalls a massacre there during the Chilean occupation of 1881 to 1883. The department, of 14,028 square miles, lies wholly in the Cordillera region.
britannica-1911-jimenes-de-cisneros-fran:
Francisco Jimenes de Cisneros, a Spanish cardinal and statesman who lived from 1436 to 1517, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Torrelaguna in Castile. His family was good but poor. He studied at Alcalá de Henares and then at Salamanca.

In 1459, having entered holy orders, he went to Rome. He came back to Spain in 1465. He brought a papal letter that gave him claim to a church post at Uzeda. He took possession of that post in 1473. The archbishop of Toledo opposed him. When Jimenes refused to give way, the archbishop threw him into prison. For six years he held out. At last, in 1480, he was restored to his post. He soon traded it for a chaplaincy at Siguenza. The article traces the hard start of a churchman who rose to rule.
britannica-1911-lecco:
Lecco, a town of Lombardy in the province of Como in Italy, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies thirty two miles by rail north by east of Milan. A steamer from Como also serves the town. It stands 673 feet above sea level, near the south end of the east branch of the Lake of Como.

That branch is often known on its own as the Lake of Lecco. Rail lines run from the town to Colico, Bergamo, and beyond. To the south a fine bridge crosses the Adda, first built in 1335 and rebuilt in 1609. For all its age, Lecco wears a modern face in its streets. Little of the old town stands save part of its castle walls. Its schools win special praise in the entry. Iron works, copper works, oil mills, and silk spinning give it trade.
britannica-1911-lopez-de-gomara-francisc:
Francisco Lopez de Gomara, a Spanish writer of the past born about fifteen ten, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was schooled at the town of Alcala, where he took holy orders. Soon after fifteen forty he joined the household of the famed Cortes. Cortes gave him most of the stuff for his books.

His History of the Indies came out in fifteen fifty two. A tale of the conquest of New Spain came the same year. Smooth style and new matter charmed the Spanish public at first. Then praise of Cortes at the cost of his men brought a sharp swing back. Both works were banned in fifteen fifty three, though French and Italian forms still spread. The entry is a sharp case of how fame and ban can sit side by side.
britannica-1911-magliabechi-antonio-da-m: Antonio da Marco Magliabechi, an Italian lover of books who lived from 1633 to 1714, is the subject of a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Florence and worked as a goldsmith in his youth. In 1673 he became keeper of books to the grand-duke of Tuscany. His own self-taught learning was vast. At his death he left his large stock of books to the grand-duke, who passed them on to the city of Florence.
britannica-1911-malleco:
Malleco is a province of southern Chile, once part of the Indian territory of Araucania. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 2,973 square miles and 98,032 people in 1895. It lies in the rainy, forested south and is thinly peopled, many of its folk being Araucanian Indians in the Andean foothills.

Gold placer mining draws some notice but yields little. The main work is raising cattle and wheat and cutting timber. The capital is Angol, a small town on the Malleco river with a station on a branch of the state railway. Traiguen in the south and Victoria to its east are the next towns of note. Victoria served for a time as the end of the main railway line.
britannica-1911-masdeu-juan-francisco:
Juan Francisco Masdeu, a Spanish historian who lived from 1744 to 1817, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Palermo and joined the Company of Jesus in December 1759. He became a professor in the Jesuit seminaries at Ferrara and Ascoli. He visited Spain in 1799, was exiled, and returned in 1815.

Masdeu died at Valencia in April 1817. His critical history of Spain and Spanish culture first came out in two volumes in the early 1780s. It grew at last into twenty volumes, and still was left unfinished at his death. On the same scale it would have run to fifty volumes in all. The entry praises his critical spirit and his rare care for accuracy. It faults him for dwelling on small details over the philosophy of history, yet calls his narrative lucid and not yet obsolete.
britannica-1911-maximilian-emperor-of-me:
Maximilian, emperor of Mexico, born at Schonbrunn in eighteen thirty two, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of an Austrian archduke. As a boy he was quick and showed a taste for art and for plant study.

He trained for the navy and rose fast to high command. He helped build the port of Trieste and its fleet. In eighteen fifty seven he was made ruler of a part of Italy held by Austria. That same year he wed a Belgian princess. He later built a fine house near Trieste. Mexican exiles first asked him to take their throne in eighteen fifty nine.
britannica-1911-minghetti-marco:
Marco Minghetti, an Italian thinker on state finance and a statesman, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bologna in eighteen eighteen, he backed reform in the papal states as a young man. He helped found a newspaper at Bologna with two partners. He also served on a council to draft a charter for those states.

In the first cabinet under that charter he held the post for public works. He quit after the pope spoke against the Italian war for freedom. He then joined the Piedmontese army as a captain on the general staff. The entry follows his path in the making of a united Italy.
britannica-1911-montefalco: Montefalco is a brief town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a town in the province of Perugia, in Italy, six miles south west of Foligno. The town stands on a hill, 1,550 feet above the sea. Its count in 1901 was 3,397 in the town. The short entry deals chiefly with art. The churches hold many works of the Umbrian school. In one church, wall paintings of 1452 show scenes from the life of Saint Francis.
britannica-1911-morocco:
Morocco, a free state of North Africa, opens a long study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its Arabic name means the Farthest West of the Moslem world. The sea bounds it north and west, Algeria east, and the Sahara south. Those land bounds can be drawn only in rough lines.

The east line with Algeria is a mere drawn line from a treaty of 1844. In 1900 France took oases in the south and bent that line west. The hold of the sultan on far tribes waxes and wanes with his power. The entry warns that Morocco is the part of North Africa least known to Europe. Its maps rest in part on guess and chance. The known part in detail is the coast, with its rough Rif hills and cliffs.
britannica-1911-pacheco-francisco:
Francisco Pacheco, a Spanish painter and art historian who lived from 1571 to 1654, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Seville in 1571. Fair samples of his style hang in the Madrid gallery. Two churches near Seville also hold his work.

Pacheco won great popularity in his city and his day. Early in the sixteen hundreds he opened an academy of painting there. The school drew large numbers of pupils to his teaching. By far the most distinguished of them was Velazquez, who later became his son-in-law. From about 1625 Pacheco gave up painting for letters and learned society. His chief book is a treatise on the art of painting, printed in 1649. The article rates it of high value for its facts on Spanish art. He died five years after it appeared.
britannica-1911-penni-gianfrancesco: Gianfrancesco Penni, in the 1911 Britannica, gets a short painter's entry covering a life from 1488 to 1528. An Italian painter born at Florence, he was surnamed Il Fattore for his close tie to Raphael. After Giulio Romano he stood as Raphael's favourite pupil. He spent his last years at Naples and worked in both oil and fresco. His name rests chiefly on his work in the Loggie of the Vatican at Rome.
britannica-1911-pernambuco:
Pernambuco, a state in north-eastern Brazil, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It is bounded by Ceará and Parahyba to the north and by the Atlantic to the east. Alagôas and Bahia lie to the south, and Piauhy to the west. The article gives its area as 49,573 square miles. Its people numbered 1,178,150 in the 1900 count.

The state has three belts of land. A narrow, low coastal zone is well wooded and fertile, with a hot, wet climate eased by trade winds. Behind it lies a drier middle zone of lighter growth, reached by terraces and slopes. The inland plateau, called the sertão, is high, stony, and dry. Long droughts often devastate that inner region. Flat-topped ranges, called chapadas, mark the borders with three states. The year splits into a rainy season and a dry one.
britannica-1911-pico:
Pico is a short place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Portuguese island in the Azores group in the Atlantic Ocean. The island held 24,028 people in 1900 and covers 175 square miles. Pico is itself a cone shaped mountain that rises to 7,612 feet, and its soil is wholly made of crushed lava. Its chief town is Lagens do Pico.

The island once made the wine called Fayal, named for a nearby island, and shipped it widely to Europe. In 1852 the Oidium fungus struck the vines and wiped them out, while a scale insect hurt the orange trees almost as badly. Hardship drove many people to emigrate in great numbers. The planting of fig trees and apricots later eased the want. The article also notes a local wood much like mahogany and equal to it in quality.
britannica-1911-pizarro-francisco:
Francisco Pizarro, conqueror of Peru, who lived from about 1471 to 1541, is profiled at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Trujillo in Spain, he was the natural son of a colonel of infantry. Little is known of his youth, and his schooling was neglected. News of the New World drew him across the Atlantic.

In 1510 Pizarro took part in a voyage to Uraba and was left in charge of a failing settlement. He marched with Balboa to the discovery of the Pacific. At Panama he became a cattle farmer on granted land. In 1522 he joined a priest and a soldier in a pact to explore south. Left for months on a small island with just thirteen men, he held on. He coasted far south and heard clear reports of the empire of Peru.
britannica-1911-pozoblanco: Pozoblanco is a town in southern Spain, in the province of Cordova. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it near the headwaters of the Guadamatillas river. It ranks among the chief towns of the Los Pedroches lowlands. No railway served the district, yet trade thrived there. Its fairs were famed for livestock and farm goods on show. Zinc and silver bearing lead mines lay nearby. Cloth and leather making gave work in the town itself.
britannica-1911-pradilla-francisco:
Francisco Pradilla, a Spanish painter born in 1847, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was born at Villanueva de Gallego, near Saragossa. He studied first at the Fernando Academy and then at the Spanish Academy in Rome. He later became director of that Roman academy. In time he rose as the leading historical painter of modern Spain. In 1896 he was made director of the Madrid Museum.

Pradilla is best known for large historical scenes. Joan the Mad won a gold medal at Paris in 1878. The Surrender of Granada won gold at Munich in 1883. In such works he dropped heavy colour for a lighter, airy key. He also painted fine genre scenes in the manner of Fortuny. His decorative work follows Tiepolo, above all in a Madrid palace. He joined the Berlin Academy in 1892.
britannica-1911-sacchetti-franco:
Franco Sacchetti is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Sacchetti was an Italian poet and tale writer who lived from about 1335 to about 1400. He was born at Florence into a noble and ancient family named in Dante. While still young he won fame as a poet. He travelled as far as Genoa and Milan on public business.

The article notes that he was spared when his house was banished in 1380. His goodness was given as the reason. He held town offices at Bibbiena, San Miniato, and Faenza.
