In 1398 his fellow citizens made him captain of their province of Romagna. His fame rests on his short tales, first printed in 1724. He wrote three hundred, of which most survive in whole or part. They draw on real life in Florence and show the manners of his age.
britannica-1911-saco:
Saco is a city in York county, Maine, on the Saco river and the sea. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it across from Biddeford, with bridges to join them. It lies 14 miles south west of Portland, the entry notes. Its count rose from 6,075 in 1890 to 6,583 in 1910. The Boston and Maine railway serves the town each day.

Town limits spread across some forty square miles of land. Much of that ground is thinly settled, the entry admits. The Dyer Library, founded in 1790, held 16,000 books in 1908. York Institute, set up in 1866, adds its own shelves of books. Thornton Academy has taught boys and girls there since 1813.
britannica-1911-san-francisco:
San Francisco is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city in California. It is the chief seaport and metropolis of the Pacific Coast. In 1910 it ranked tenth in population in the United States. It was the largest city west of the Missouri river. It sits at the end of a peninsula. The ocean lies on one side of it. The Bay of San Francisco lies on the other.

Counts show its fast growth over sixty years. It held 34,000 people in 1850 by the text's count. By 1910 that count had reached 416,912. Many of its people were foreign born at that date. The peninsula within city limits is six to eight miles broad. The bay runs some fifty miles in its medial line. Its shoreline runs to more than three hundred miles. Its area is about 450 square miles in all.
britannica-1911-stucco:
Stucco is the subject of a brief building entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from Italian, adapted from an old German word for crust or piece. It names a kind of plaster used to cover walls. It is also used for trim features such as cornices and mouldings, and for ceilings.

The entry draws a clear line between two grades of the material. The stucco used as an outer coat on brick or stone work is coarse. A finer kind is used for ornamental work inside and out. Readers are sent to the entry on plaster work for the fuller account of how such materials are made and applied.
britannica-1911-suarez-francisco:
Francisco Suarez, a Spanish theologian and philosopher who lived from 1548 to 1617, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Granada, he was educated at Salamanca. Under the sway of a Jesuit teacher, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1564. He then taught philosophy at Segovia and theology in several cities, including Rome.

After his doctor's degree, King Philip the Second named him chief professor of theology at Coimbra. The entry calls him almost the last great figure of scholastic thought. In doctrine he held to a moderate Thomism. On the question of universals he sought a middle course between two extremes. Only the single thing, he held, has true and real unity in the world.
britannica-1911-subiaco:
Subiaco is a town of Italy, in the province of Rome, and a gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its site and old name. The town stands on the right bank of the Anio river. It lies forty seven miles east of Rome by rail. It sits 1,339 feet above the sea, in a fine setting.

Its count in 1901 was 7,076 in the town and 8,003 in the commune. Ironworks and paper mills give the town its work. The ancient name was Sublaqueum, from its place under three lakes. Those lakes were made by art in the gorge of the Anio. They served the aqueduct of the Anio Novus, which drew its water there. On the bank of that lake, Nero built a villa for himself. A famed statue of a kneeling youth was found in its remains.
britannica-1911-tobacco:
Tobacco is the leaf of plants grown for smoking, chewing, and snuff. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with its spread from America. The leaf ranks as the most used drug plant in the world. Its use reached all other lands from the New World.

Men sent out by Columbus in 1492 saw Cubans with lit firebrands. They told of herbs carried to scent and smoke themselves. A friar on the next voyage described snuff taking in detail. Chewing was first seen on the South American coast in 1502. Smoking proved an old and wide custom across the Americas. Rites and feasts often turned on its use there. The plant itself reached Europe in 1558 with a Spanish doctor.
britannica-1911-verdi-giuseppe-fortunino:
Giuseppe Verdi, an Italian composer who lived from 1813 to 1901, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born on October 10, 1813, at Le Roncole, a poor village near Busseto. His parents kept a small inn and shop. A merchant of Busseto took him in and gave his music a true start.

Verdi wrote marches and band pieces for his town as a boy, and a first symphony at age fifteen. Milan's school turned him down in 1832, so he studied with a private teacher. Back in Busseto he led the town band and played the church organ. His first opera, Oberto, was staged at Milan in 1839. A comic opera then failed as he lost his wife and two children.
britannica-1911-white-joseph-blanco:
Joseph Blanco White, a British theologian and poet who lived from 1775 to 1841, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Seville on 11 July 1775, he was educated for the Roman Catholic priesthood. After his ordination in 1800, religious doubts led him to flee Spain for England in 1810. There he entered the Anglican Church in time.

White studied theology at Oxford and made the friendship of Arnold, Newman, and Whately there. He became tutor in the family of Whately when that man was made archbishop of Dublin in 1831. While in that post he embraced Unitarian views in his faith. He then found an asylum among the Unitarians of Liverpool, where he died in 1841. White edited a monthly Spanish magazine in London from 1810 to 1814.
britannica-1911-yauco:
Yauco is a city in the district of Ponce on the island of Porto Rico, west of the city that gives the district its name. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its town count from the census at the close of the past age, about six thousand souls. A rail line of the island serves the city.

The entry sets Yauco on high ground with a fine, mild air. A wagon road links it to its port town, which has a first rate harbor for ships. Coffee and tobacco are the chief trades of the place. The piece closes with a single date from its past: the town was first settled in the mid seventeen hundreds, in the years of Spanish rule.
britannica-1911-zurbaran-francisco:
Francisco Zurbaran is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Zurbaran was a Spanish painter who lived from 1598 to 1662. He was born at Fuente de Cantos, a son of a country labourer. As a child he copied objects in charcoal. His father sent him young to a painting school in Seville. He soon became the best pupil there, passing his master.

The article says he gained the name of the Spanish Caravaggio for his strong, true to life style. He painted direct from nature and used a lay figure to study cloth. He had a special gift for white cloth, so monks fill many of his works. Near 1630 the king made him his painter. His career stayed in Spain and passed with few events beyond daily work. He died in Madrid, probably in 1662.
by-right-of-conquest-or-with-cortez-in-m:
G. A. Henty wrote a boys' tale of the fall of Mexico, with twenty-two chapters and a preface. The preface sets the wonder plain. A vast realm, full of warlike folk, fell to a mere handful of Spaniards. No tale maker would dare such a plot, Henty holds. Brave men and better arms tell part of it.

A stark offer and a start for unknown parts open the run. Voyage, isles, and wreck lead to Anahuac. A fine land, Tezcuco, and life in a palace fill the first ashore part. Cortez steps in at the eleventh chapter. Flight, the Cholula killings, and entry to Mexico mark the heart. Treasure room, revolt, and the causeway fight fill the late run. A victim for the gods and a road home close the list. One lad's eyes carry the great clash for young readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-de-maris:
Adam de Marisco, or Adam Marsh, was a Franciscan probably from Somerset, whose birth date is unknown. He died at the end of 1257 or start of 1258. Educated at Oxford, where he won a great reputation, he had served three years as Wearmouth's rector in Durham before joining the Friars Minor about 1237. At the Oxford Franciscan house he succeeded Robert Grosseteste as lecturer.

His correspondence shows how wide his personal influence ran. It illustrates the moral force of the early Franciscans in England. Intimate with Grosseteste, Archbishop Boniface, Richard of Cornwall, and Simon de Montfort, he helped give Earl Simon his deep interest in reform. He died just as the great crisis of Henry III's reign began. Roger Bacon called him and Grosseteste the greatest clerks in the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-steu:
Agostino Steuco, Steuchus, was an exegete born at Gubbio, Umbria, in 1496. He died at Venice in 1549. At seventeen he joined the Lateran Canons Regular at Gubbio. In 1525 he became director of Cardinal Grimani's library at Venice; in 1530, prior of Reggio's canons. Early in 1538 Paul III appointed him Bishop of Kisamos in Crete.

Paul III also put him over the Vatican Library on 27 October of the same year, though in that post he did not accomplish much. In 1547 Paul III made him legate to the Tridentine Council, transferred to Bologna; he died returning to Rome. A man of varied talents, he knew history, philosophy, and theology well, with Greek and Hebrew. His chiefly exegetical works appeared in three volumes from Ambrogio Morando, Paris 1578 and Venice 1591 and 1601.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-amico: Antonio Amico, a canon of Palermo who died in 1641, wrote church history for Syracuse and Messina. His works also covered Sicily's kings and admirals. The same short entry adds Bernardino, a Neapolitan Franciscan who died in 1590. As prior at Jerusalem he wrote a 1609 treatise on the plans and images of the holy buildings there, illustrated by Callot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-and-leo:
Carlo Marenco was an Italian dramatist born at Cassolo in Piedmont in 1800 who died at Savona in 1846. After studying law he chose literature, supporting himself with a Treasury post at Savona. A Romantic, he rejected the unity of time and gave his plots fuller development than classic rules allowed. His figures feel alive and his diction is polished, though his tragedies lean toward the sentimental.

Dante inspired several of his tragedies, including Pia de' Tolomei, Corso Donati, and Conte Ugolino, beside historical plays such as Arnoldo da Brescia and Corradino. His son Leopoldo, born at Ceva in 1831 and dead in 1899, followed him into the Treasury and then into drama, teaching Latin literature from 1860. Leopoldo's many plays, from Celeste and Saffo to Piccarda Donati, also draw on Dante and on modern and medieval history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuzco:
A diocesan entry sketches Cuzco, a suffragan see of Lima in Peru. The city, capital of its department, lies 11,000 feet above sea level on the eastern end of the Knot of Cuzco. The original Inca city, reputedly founded in the eleventh century and destroyed by Pizarro in 1535. Remains of the Inca palace, the Temple of the Sun, and the Temple of the Virgins of the Sun survive.

Among the finest later buildings stands Santo Domingo cathedral. The diocese, erected by Paul III in 1536, covers Cuzco and Apurimac. It spans 21,677 square miles, with a Catholic population of 480,000. It counted 106 parishes, 650 churches and chapels, 150 priests, a seminary, and schools at the time of writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durango-mexic:
Durango in Mexico is an archdiocese in the northwest of the country. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry dates its founding to 28 September 1620. Seventy-two years earlier, friars Diego de la Cadena and Geronimo de Mendoza had founded a mission in the Sierra Madre valley, San Juan Bautista de Analco. Captain Ibarra of Spain founded the city itself in 1554, and missionaries made it their hub at once.

Their work among the natives bore such fruit that under Philip the Third, Guadalajara was split by Paul the Fifth and Durango rose to episcopal rank. Its first bishop, Gonzalo Hernandez y Hermosillo, gave much time to the Indians' welfare. At first the diocese held New Mexico, Chihuahua, and Sonora, later made sees of their own. The city, also called Guadiana, stands at sixty-seven hundred feet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-el-greco:
El Greco was one of the most striking Spanish painters, born in Crete between 1545 and 1550 and dead at Toledo in 1614. In 1570 the miniaturist Giulio Clovio wrote to Cardinal Farnese praising him as a Cretan then at Rome who had studied under Titian. Yet El Greco took little from Titian, and his work stands apart, with only traces of Bassano, Baroccio, Veronese, and Tintoretto.

He reached Spain in 1577, signed his name in Greek letters, and always called himself a Cretan. At Toledo in 1582 he spoke before the Inquisition as interpreter for a countryman accused of being a Moor, and there he settled for good. Famed for cold blue tones, greys, and many whites, he painted in a manner that looked ahead by a century and a half. His greatest work is the Burial of the Count of Orgaz in the church of Santo Tome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filippo-brune:
Filippo Brunellesco was a Florentine architect and sculptor born in 1377 and dead in 1446. Trained first as a goldsmith, he turned to sculpture and then gave himself wholly to architecture. He was among the chief leaders of the early Renaissance in architecture. He first applied the rules of perspective to art in a set, reasoned form.

His crowning work was the dome of Florence cathedral, which he raised without centering. The dome used pointed octagonal arches and a double shell, with stairs and passages between them. A lantern crowned the dome and added sixteen metres to its height of ninety-one metres. He also built the sacristy dome of San Lorenzo and the charming freestanding Pazzi Chapel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fra-angelico:
Fra Angelico, born Guido di Pietro near Vicchio in Tuscany in 1387 and dead at Rome in 1455, was a Dominican friar. He was one of the most beloved painters of the Florentine school. He joined the Dominicans at Fiesole in 1407 with his brother Benedetto. He began as an illuminator of missals and choir books, and grew into a painter of religious scenes marked by simple naturalness and deep piety.

His best-known work is the fresco cycle in the convent of San Marco in Florence, alongside Madonnas, a Coronation of the Virgin, and an Adoration of the Magi. Frescoes on the lives of St. Lawrence and St. Stephen fill the Chapel of St. Nicholas in the Vatican. His technique was slender by later standards, but the entry presents his gentle, prayerful art as the reason his name endures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-ami:
Francesco Amico, born at Cosenza on 2 April 1578, was one of the great theologians of his age and a Jesuit of profound humility. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1596, taught theology for twenty-four years at Naples, Aquila, and Gratz, and spent five years as chancellor of the academy at Gratz. His method was scholastic, shaped to fit a four-year course of teaching, and his doctrine is described as following St. Thomas, brief, clear, subtle, and solid.

His works cover God one and three, the nature of angels, the last end, faith, hope, and charity, and justice and right, besides the Incarnation and the sacraments. One treatise, on justice and right, was banned in 1651 until corrected, because of three propositions objected to by Popes Alexander VII and Innocent XI. A corrected edition of 1649 was allowed. The entry ranks him among the foremost Jesuit theologians of the seventeenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francescoe-de:
Francesco de Vico, born at Macerata on 19 May 1805 and dead at London on 15 November 1848. He was a Jesuit astronomer who gave the Roman College observatory a European reputation. Entering the Society of Jesus at Sant' Andrea in Rome, he showed a gift for mathematics and astronomy and became professor of those subjects. He assisted director Father Dumouchel, and succeeded him as director in 1839.

He won the French Academy's Lalande prizes and six times took the King of Denmark's gold medal for the first discovery of a telescopic comet. One medal now rests in the museum at Georgetown University. Driven from Rome by the political disturbances of 1848, he was invited by Arago to stay in Paris. He chose Georgetown College's new observatory instead, reaching America on 22 July 1848. He died at London that November, on his way, still at work for the science he loved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Franco, often called Il Semolei, was an Italian historical painter and etcher born at Udine in 1510, who died at Venice in 1580. He studied at Rome with close attention to Michelangelo, favoring large allegorical decorations. A Catholic Encyclopedia article remembers him less for painting than for his etchings, of which more than a hundred survive.

He worked with Vasari on decorations for Ottaviano de' Medici, and painted portraits of the Medici family, largely copies from other men. His designs for majolica for the Duke of Urbino mattered in their day. His plates, signed B.F.V.F., run somewhat mechanical in execution, yet carry a light, easy spirit. About half are original, while the rest follow Raphael, Titian, and others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-lanf:
Giovanni Lanfranco, also known as Cavaliere Giovanni di Stefano, was a decorative painter born at Parma in 1581, who died at Rome in 1647. As a boy page at Piacenza he showed a talent for drawing and was placed under Agostino Carracci. Before sixteen he had painted a Virgin and Saints admired enough for Sant' Agostino at Piacenza. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a bold rival of Domenichino.

After Carracci's death he assisted Annibale Carracci in the Farnese Gallery and Roman churches. By scheming he won a commission promised to Domenichino. In the cupola of Sant' Andrea della Valle he painted his greatest work, the Virgin seated in clouds, grand and daring in design and coloring. At Naples he finished Domenichino's treasury cupola, destroying most of his rival's work, and Urban VIII later knighted him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-huanuco:
Huánuco is a suffragan diocese of Lima in Peru. Its department covers over fourteen thousand square miles with a population of about one hundred and forty-five thousand in 1896. The capital, also called San León de Huánuco, stands on the upper Huallaga, a tributary of the Amazon, nearly six thousand feet above sea level, with about seven thousand five hundred people.

Huánuco ranks among Peru's oldest Spanish colonies, founded in 1539 by Gómez de Alvarado at Pizarro's instance, four years after Lima. Indians levelled the first houses in revolt, and after Pizarro's murder a new colony entered the valley. Silver mines at Cerro de Pasco once raised the city to a reported seventy thousand people, but nineteenth-century wars reduced it to a scattered town living chiefly on fruit farming.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignatius-pers:
Ignatius Persico was an Italian cardinal, born at Naples in 1823 and dead in 1896. He joined the Capuchin Franciscans in 1839, and right after ordination was sent in 1846 to Patna in India. Anastasius Hartmann, the vicar apostolic, took him as companion and confidant. In 1850 Persico followed Hartmann to Bombay, helping found a seminary and the Bombay Catholic Examiner.

During the Goanese schism of 1853, the bishop dispatched Persico to Rome and London to put the Catholic case to pope and British government, winning British recognition for Catholic rights. Consecrated bishop in 1854, he served as auxiliary to Hartmann, then as visitor of Agra and vicar apostolic there. During the Indian Mutiny his life was repeatedly in danger, and failing health forced his return to Italy in 1860. Later missions took him to America and Baltimore's council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joannes-de-sa:
Joannes de Sacrobosco, or John Holywood, was an English-born monk and astronomy professor at Paris during the thirteenth century's first half, dead there in 1256. His Latin name likely renders Holywood, whether in Yorkshire, near Dublin, or in Nithsdale, Scotland, and he studied at Oxford before teaching in France.

Sacrobosco won fame through De Sphaera, a short textbook of spherical astronomy written because Ptolemy and others daunted beginners. Used at universities for centuries, it ran to nearly a hundred editions before the mid-seventeenth century, first printed at Ferrara in 1472. Brevity and clarity made it the standard gateway to the stars until Copernicus won general assent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-selgas-y:
José Selgas y Carrasco was a Spanish poet and novelist who lived from 1824 to 1882. Born at Lorca in Murcia, he trained at the Seminary of San Fulgencio but cut his studies short to help support his family. In Madrid he held minor government posts, wrote journalism, and served as secretary to Prime Minister Martínez Campos. The Spanish Academy elected him a member.

His reputation rests on lyrics and short tales rather than his longer novels, which the entry calls rather tedious. His best verse, marked by a gentle sadness, appears in La Primavera and El Estio, both from 1850. A staunch conservative, he attacked liberals in the press, and his tales swing between sentiment and a darker, at times morbid, pessimism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-conchill:
Juan Conchillos Falco was a Valencian painter remembered for humor and kindliness. Born at Valencia in 1641 to an old noble family, he studied under the eccentric Esteban March and became one of the first Spanish artists to run a school of design. He made pupils work in charcoal to gain freedom of draftsmanship.

Falco was a brilliant sketcher whose roadside drawings of travel scenes show wit, a rare gift among Spanish painters of his age. His chief works adorn San Salvador in Valencia, with an Immaculate Conception for the Franciscans and frescoes at San Juan. Struck by palsy late in life, he became a cripple, lost his sight, and died blind in 1711.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mameluco:
Mameluco comes from the Arabic memluk, meaning slave, once the household cavalry of Egypt's sultans, drawn largely from children of Christian slaves. In South America the word took a wider sense. It named the mixed European and Indian race, and more sharply the organised Portuguese slave-hunting bands of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

Those bands ravaged the interior from the Atlantic to the Andes and from Paraguay to the Orinoco. Enslavement began almost with discovery, urged by Columbus as early as 1493 and denounced by Dominicans in Hispaniola in 1511. Brazilian settlers, already Europe's professional slave dealers, married into wild tribes and bred the hardy, cruel Mamelucos. From Sao Paulo and Para, from about 1560, they raided for nearly two centuries. In 1629 Paulista armies smashed the Guarani missions of Paraguay, wrecking all but two of twelve missions and hauling away 60,000 Christian Indians to sell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mexico:
Mexico, a diocese whose bounds were at first ill defined, stretches in the entry across two heads: boundaries and bishops. When Cuba was found, three sees were raised, but when the prelates arrived, their sees were destroyed and the people fled. From 1500 to 1863 the Diocese of Mexico ran from Atlantic to Pacific, Tampico to Acapulco.

Today it covers the Federal District, the States of Morelos and Mexico, and part of Hidalgo. The first bishop, Zumarraga, reached Mexico just as Clement VII left Castel Sant' Angelo prison, where Charles V had kept him months after Bourbon's sack of Rome. Allowed, even obliged, to come on the emperor's nomination alone, Zumarraga ruled without papal appointment, styling himself Omnimoda potestate Antistes. He returned to Spain, gained his bulls, and was consecrated six years after first landing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-morocco:
Morocco, named for Marrakesh, forms Africa's northwest corner. It is separated from French Algeria by an imaginary line some 217 miles long, and answers to the Roman Mauretania Tingitana. Natives call it Gharb, the West, or Magreb el Aksa, the Extreme West. It spans a little over 308,000 square miles with about 10,000,000 people.

Three parallel mountain chains break its surface. The Great Atlas plateau bears snow-clad peaks of 10,000 to 13,000 feet. The Riff faces the Mediterranean above the fertile Tell, and the arid Sahara lies to the south. Except for Abyssinia it was then Africa's only independent native state. The sultan's writ ran thin beyond the Bled el Makhzen, the tax-paying country, while the Bled es Siba stayed unsubdued. The entry follows its missions and church life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-mexico:
New Mexico, in January 1911 a United States territory awaiting only its Constitution's completion and federal acceptance to rank as a state, lies between 31 and 37 degrees north. It extends from 103 to 109 degrees west. Colorado bounds it in the north, Oklahoma and Texas in the east, Texas and Mexico in the south, and Arizona in the west. It spans about 370 miles east to west and 335 north to south, covering 122,580 square miles.

Mountain, plateau and valley flank the Rio Grande on either side. Average rainfall is 12 inches, usually July to September, so spring and summer run dry and farming and grazing suffer. Climate is uniform, summers moderate, and dry air keeps heat from oppressing. Winters run long but not severe in the northwest and northeast, short and mild further south. The 1900 census counted 141,282 people, 33 percent illiterate; 1910 counted 327,296, about half of Spanish descent. The entry covers soil, mines, towns, and Church missions and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nusco: Nusco, a diocese in Avellino province suffragan to Salerno, dates from the eleventh century and counts 19 parishes with 38,300 people. Its bishops include Guido in 1004, Saint Amatus, historian of the Normans, Roger, who restored the cathedral, and Cardinal Parisio, who presided at Trent, with Montemartino united to the see in 1820. Its first bishop of Montemartino, Saint John, dates to 1084.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-de-anaz:
Pedro de Anazco was born at Chachapoyas in Peru in 1550 and dead at Asuncion in Paraguay in 1605. His father was Pedro de Anazco, a Spanish captain, companion of Belalcazar in Ecuador's conquest, through whom, it is said, first notice of Guatavita's Dorado reached Spaniards in Ecuador. At twenty-two Anazco became a Jesuit. In 1577 he was sent to Juli on Lake Titicaca. Thence he moved on to the Chaco tribe among the Abipones and, in 1593, to Paraguay, where he died.

He was an untiring missionary and zealous student of Indian tongues. Highly respected authorities like Gonzalez Davila and Lozano credit him with grammars, doctrines, and catechisms in nine different South American Indian languages. None of Anazco's linguistic works have been published, and most, if not all, his manuscripts are feared lost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-principality-:
Monaco sits on the Mediterranean, on the skirts of the Turbie and Tête de Chien mountains. The French department of the Maritime Alps rings it on all sides, over an area of 5,337 acres. Its chief resources are the gulf fishery, fruit trees, and the Monte Carlo Casino, raised in 1856, whose revenues free the folk from taxation.

The capital holds three great boroughs: old Monaco, built on a promontory running 875 yards into the sea and ringing the harbour, plus Condamine and Monte Carlo.  Notable works include the old fortifications and the old ducal palace, whose frescoes come from Annibale Carracci, Orazio Ferrari, and Carlone. The cathedral, raised in 1884 to 1887 in Byzantine style under Prince Albert III, the Casino, and the great fountain of the public square also stand out. Monaco dates from Phoenician times, when a temple to Melkarth, called Monoicos, stood on the old town's promontory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-puerto-rico:
Puerto Rico, smallest and most easterly of the Greater Antilles, fills a long encyclopedia entry. It covers 3,670 square miles. It counted 1,118,012 people in the census of 1910, over 304 to the square mile. That was a growth of 125,769 in ten years. Columbus sighted its north-east mountain, El Yunque, on 16 November 1493, and his fleet anchored near Aguadilla. A monument marks where he took possession, naming the island San Juan.

Church and state relations take the second half, through three concordats between the Holy See and the kings of Spain. The first dates to 13 May 1418, between Martin the Fifth and John the Second of Castile. The second, between Philip the Fifth and Innocent the Thirteenth, led to the agreement of 2 January 1753. Benedict the Fourteenth and Ferdinand the Sixth made that agreement. It ruled church-state relations in Spain and her colonies until Ferdinand the Seventh died in 1833.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-francisco:
San Francisco, an archdiocese erected on 29 July 1853, first covered thirteen California counties north of 37 degrees 5 minutes, some 16,856 square miles. Monterey and Los Angeles, Sacramento, and Salt Lake served as suffragans. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces California's church from Spanish missions to a modern province.

All California once formed the diocese of Both Californias under Francisco Garcia Diego y Moreno. Franciscans landing with Cortés at Santa Cruz Bay in 1535 began the first mission work under Martín de la Coruña. The entry follows the mission chain, the American takeover, the gold rush growth, and the building of parishes, schools, and seminaries that turned a mission frontier into a metropolitan see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-fe-new-:
Santa Fe in America, an archdiocese in New Mexico, was erected by Pius IX in 1850 and raised to an archbishopric in 1875. At first it covered New Mexico, Colorado, and Arizona, detached from Durango in Mexico, but since 1868 it has held only the larger part of New Mexico. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes a missionary archdiocese.

About 150,000 Catholics lived there, including 12,000 Pueblo Indians of the Tiguex and Quirix peoples, with most of the rest of Spanish descent. Fifty parish churches and 350 mission chapels, mostly built or repaired since 1852, were served by seventy priests, fifty secular and twenty regular. Each priest rode a circuit of six to ten scattered missions, and only one priest in the whole archdiocese was native-born.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebenico:
Sebenico, suffragan of Zara, was a bishop's seat before it became a see. When its people could not get on with their bishop at Trau, they chose bishops of their own. Fifty years later the energetic Boniface VIII founded the see and named the Franciscan Sisgorich first bishop. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a self-willed Dalmatian town.

Work on the cathedral began in 1443, though consecration waited a century. The Dominican bishop Vincenzo Arrigoni served the see well, holding seven synods between 1602 and 1626. John Berzich attended the Vienna synod in 1849, and Johann Zaffron served as father of the council at the Vatican Council. Despite gains from Scardona in 1813 and parts of Trau and Tinin in 1828, Sebenico counts only 93,000 Catholics with fifty-four priests, eighty-three friars, and sixty-eight nuns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-silvio-pellic:
Silvio Pellico, Italian author and patriot, was born at Saluzzo on 24 June 1788 and died at Turin on 31 January 1854. His father worked for the government, and Silvio spent his youth across Italy, with four years at Lyons. At twenty he was in Milan, meeting Monti, Foscolo, and Manzoni. He taught French in a government school for soldiers' orphans, then tutored privately for Count Luigi Porro Lambertenghi, a leading foe of Austrian rule.

Lambertenghi founded Il Conciliatore in 1819, a journal that voiced Romantic doctrines and fought foreign domination of Italy. Pellico helped edit it. In 1820, suspected as a Carbonaro with Pietro Maroncelli, he was arrested by the Austrians and held in Venice's Piombi and Murano's dungeon. Condemned to death, then reprieved to hard labor, he was taken to the Spielberg fortress in Moravia, whose sufferings made his prison memoirs famous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-clare-of-m:
St. Clare of Montefalco was born at Montefalco about 1268 and died there on 18 August 1308. This entry follows a life much disputed as to whether Clare was a Franciscan or an Augustinian. Wadding, with Franciscan biographers, contends she joined the Third Order of St. Francis. Augustinian writers — favoured, it seems, by the Bollandists — hold she belonged to their order.

It seems more probable, however, that Clare, when still a very young girl, embraced the secular rule of the Third Order of St. Francis. She did so with her older sister and other pious young maidens, who wore the Third Order habit and followed the communal mode of life their piety and fervour suggested. When later they desired to enter the religious state in its strict sense and profess the three vows of religion, they petitioned the Spoleto bishop for admission to a stricter rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-bosco:
John Bosco, founder of the Salesians, grew from a Piedmont shepherd boy into Turin's apostle of youth. Born in a cabin at Becchi near Castelnuovo on 16 August 1815 to poor parents, he lost his father past age two, leaving Margaret Bosco to raise three boys. He herded sheep, learned first lessons from his parish priest, and showed ready wit and retentive memory. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 31 January 1888.

Poverty often pulled him from books to field, but longing for study never left him. In 1835 he entered Chieri seminary, and after six years Archbishop Franzoni of Turin ordained him priest on Trinity Sunday's eve. At Turin he threw himself into priestly labour among the young, and from that work grew the Salesian Society. Pius X declared him Venerable in 1907, and a later note records Pius XI's beatification in 1929 and canonization in 1934.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-nola:
Peter Nolasco, founder of the Mercedarians, gave his fortune and his order to ransoming Christian captives. Born near Castelnaudary in France in 1189 or 1182, he was noted from youth for piety, almsgiving, and charity. He spent his patrimony freeing captives held by the Moors, then took a vow of virginity and moved to Barcelona.

Moved by a heavenly vision and encouraged by Raymond of Peñafort and James I of Aragon, he founded his order in 1218 for the redemption of slaves. Gregory IX approved it in 1230. Its members vowed to spend all their substance on ransoms and, if need be, to stay in captivity themselves in a captive's place. He died at Barcelona on Christmas Day 1256 or 1259.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-subiaco:
Subiaco, a city twenty-five miles from Tivoli in the Province of Rome, takes its name from the lakes of Nero's villa. It is famed for the sacred grotto called Sagro Speco, the Abbey of St Scholastica, and the hilltop church of St Andrew. Benedict, aged fourteen, lived three years in a cave above the Anio, fed by the monk Roman, and that grotto became the cradle of the Benedictine Order.

Benedict built twelve monasteries with twelve monks each. The grotto house soon faded, was renovated in 854, again in 1053, and became a yearly procession goal under Abbot John V. A community of twelve became a priory under Innocent III, and Pius X granted a daily indulgence to pilgrims there in 1909. The abbey below, built about 520, completes the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tabasco-mexic:
Tabasco is a Mexican diocese, suffragan of Yucatán, covering the state of Tabasco, 10,872 square miles with 183,805 people in 1910. Bishop and governor live at San Juan Bautista, founded in 1598 as Villa de Felipe II, called Villa Hermosa until 1826. A decree of Charles V in 1525 already assigned Tabasco's territory to the bishopric of Yucatán and Santa Maria de los Remedios.

Dominicans passing to Chiapas in 1545 reached Tabasco, and in 1578 they organized Oxolotlán under Tomás Aguilar. Philip II planned a see, Philip III tried in 1609, and another attempt failed in 1680, until Leo XIII created the diocese in 1880 from Chiapas, Oaxaca, and Yucatán parishes. It answered to Mexico until 1891, to Oaxaca until 1906, and then to Yucatán, counting a seminary, seven parish schools, and four Catholic colleges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tricarico:
A diocese in the province of Potenza, in the Basilicata of southern Italy, near the River Perrola. In 1694 it was almost destroyed by an earthquake, and its cathedral, erected in 968 by Polyeuctos, Patriarch of Constantinople, still anchors a see whose early Greek-rite bishops are unknown by name.

After the Norman conquest the first Latin bishop was Arnoldo, in 1068, followed by theologians such as Palmerio di Gallusio in 1253. Cardinal Pier Luigi Caraffa, bishop from 1624, restored the cathedral and founded the seminary. The diocese is suffragan of Acerenza and Matera, and counts 25 parishes, 80,540 souls and 180 clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zamora-mexico:
Zamora (Mexico) is the diocese covering almost half of Michoacán state for 400,000 people. Its city, founded in 1540 by Antonio de Mendoza with fortifications as a barrier against Chichimec raids, holds 14,000 people. Vasco de Quiroga, first Bishop of Michoacán, made Zamora a parish under a rector, on ground where Franciscans had baptized Indians years before. When Michoacán became an archbishopric, Zamora took an episcopal see over the state's mountainous part.

The diocese runs two seminaries with 288 students, 159 parish schools, and twelve Catholic colleges with about eleven thousand pupils, while Protestants hold neither churches nor colleges there. A new cathedral rises in Zamora city, birthplace of Archbishop Labastida y Dávalos of Mexico. Uruapan, founded by Franciscan Juan de San Miguel among Mexico's first friars, belongs to the diocese. Its sources are Vera's geographic-historical catechism of the Mexican Church of 1881.
dave-darrin-s-third-year-at-annapolis-or:
The third year at Annapolis fills this 1911 Dave Darrin book by H. Irving Hancock. Dave and Dan now lead as second class midshipmen. Twenty-four chapters carry the year from a balked brigade to the close.

Navy football fills much of the middle, with a band that could not make itself heard. Jetson draws the hate of a rival and stands before the class meeting as a jury. Dave stands on principle more than once, and friends beg him not to be a fool. Leave to go ashore must be pled before the officer in charge. The book treats rank, sport, and honour as one lesson, in Hancock's steady series style.
doe-osti-17076873-evaluation-of-the-grai:
Katherine Montoya, Bryan Conry, Wesley Jones, and colleagues at Oak Ridge measured grain growth in zirconium carbide coatings in report ORNL/TM-2025/4139, dated September 2025. Such coatings are proposed to shield fuel particles in nuclear thermal rockets, where they must endure hot hydrogen. If grains grow too fast at heat, the shield can weaken.

Stand in coated particles were heated at 1,900 degrees Celsius for up to 300 minutes. Microscopy and diffraction mapped grain size and boundary types before and after, and Raman readings tracked carbon content. Samples began with like grain sizes, but those with more localized excess carbon kept smaller grains and grew more slowly at full heat.
doe-osti-2573763-ring-electron-cooler-fo:
Brookhaven technical note BNL-228463-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-128, summarizes feasibility studies for a Ring Electron Cooler for the Electron-Ion Collider. S. Seletskiy, J. Kewisch, Y. Jing, A. Fedotov, and D. Kayran of Brookhaven wrote it with J. Unger and G. Hoffstaetter of Cornell; the paper is dated August 6, 2025. Cooling counters the emittance growth that intrabeam scattering causes in protons at top energy.

The design stores electron bunches in a dedicated ring for several seconds, reusing the same bunches turn after turn against the hadron beam. The electrons are non-magnetized, following the approach proven at the Low Energy RHIC Electron Cooler in 2019 to 2021 runs. Damping wigglers shed the heat that scattering pumps in, preserving the electron beam's quality. Listed parameters give cooling times of two hours across and three hours along the beam, judged adequate against the scattering growth.
doe-osti-2575287-shielding-the-quantum-r:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/3912, by Robert Root, Mark Provo, and Jason Jarnagin in July 2025, argues that quantum research facilities need to police their radio frequency environment. Quantum computers, sensors, and communication systems are exquisitely sensitive to stray electromagnetic signals. Interference can corrupt experiments, and signals leaking out can compromise security, yet few facilities treat the spectrum around their labs as managed infrastructure.

The report proposes a framework with four habits: identify the RF threats and sensitivities, mitigate them, monitor the environment continuously, and audit the results. Background chapters survey qubit types and the facility systems, such as SCADA controls and internet-of-things devices, that both emit and receive signals. The authors stress teamwork among researchers, engineers, and security specialists. Their goal is best practices that keep quantum systems running with integrity while the technology and its threat landscape keep changing.
doe-osti-2587349-conceptual-design-of-th:
H Oh of Brookhaven National Laboratory wrote this technical note, BNL-228845-2025-TECH, in September 2025 on the beam abort system for the Electron Storage Ring of the Electron-Ion Collider. E Aschenauer, K Drees, and colleagues share credit for the design work. The abort system is a machine protection device: when something fails, it must throw the whole electron beam into a dump before the beam can damage the ring.

The storage ring will run electrons at 5, 10, and 18 gigaelectronvolts. The 10 gigaelectronvolt setup stores the most energy, 320 kilojoules, and the dump must absorb that within one revolution, about 20 microseconds. Two candidate designs are compared in full. One reuses a Lambertson magnet already in RHIC inventory, yawed about 15 degrees and running at 0.95 tesla. The other builds a new septum magnet. The comparison supports the project's record of decision.
doe-osti-2589001-user-manual-for-the-the:
Zhaopeng Zhong and Micheal Smith of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this user manual, ANL/NSE-25/68, for SE2RCT, a thermal hydraulic code with a narrow and important job. SE2RCT is a special version of SE2-ANL, itself a modified SUPERENERGY-2, built for models of the Experimental Breeder Reactor-II, the landmark sodium-cooled test reactor.

The code plugs into the Fuels Irradiation and Physics Database and its Physics and Analysis DataBase, the archive supporting metallic fuel research for sodium fast reactors. Where its parent code dehomogenizes pin power internally, SE2RCT takes pin power details directly from the RCT physics calculations. It returns detailed axial distributions of temperature and results. It also computes the axial distribution of displacements per atom in cladding, a key damage measure. The manual documents features, limitations, and input and output specifications, closing what the authors call the quality assurance gap of missing documentation.
doe-osti-2589287-initial-user-study-insi:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory technical report LBNL-2001682, by Drew Paine, Johanna Cohoon, and Lavanya Ramakrishnan, reports an early user study for the HPDF project. The study was published in July 2025 through the University of California. Contributors also came from Jefferson Lab and other project partners. The team asked future users what a shared data service must do for them.

Interview findings clarified community requirements and gathered first reactions to a draft design. Users wanted to search data sets held at separate facilities as if they were one collection. They also wanted to run analysis jobs on data found that way, across instruments and sites. The report records those needs in users' own words. Planners can use it to test later design choices against what the community actually asked for.
doe-osti-2589781-a-pressure-swing-proces:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory report NREL/TP-5100-94958, by Anh To, Wilson McNeary, Martha Arellano-Trevino, and co-authors, designs a one-material route from smokestack carbon dioxide to methanol. Dual functional materials hold two kinds of active sites side by side: basic sites that catch carbon dioxide and metal sites that convert it with hydrogen. Keeping the sites close is the core bet.

The process swings pressure in a fixed bed to catch, then convert, in mild conditions meant to cut plant cost. Target hosts are gas-fired power plants, where standard capture runs about 43 to 89 dollars per ton. Each plant emits about 0.47 million tons a year, but more than 1,100 such plants exist. First installation could match today's full renewable methanol output of 0.2 million tons a year.
doe-osti-2997961-vertical-characterizati:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38403, by Rebecka Iveson, Robert Mackley, and Frederick Day-Lewis, dated September 2025, looks down inside Hanford's new groundwater extraction wells. Pump-and-treat cleanup works best when wells pull hardest from the zones holding the most contamination. Standard wells are screened along the whole aquifer, so operators cannot tell which depth delivers the pollution.

Downhole flow sensors profiled flow and concentration by depth during pumping. In one zone, the upper coarse unit, stronger pumping raised the computed hydraulic conductivity values. Bypass flow, water sneaking around the sensor through the filter pack or past its sealing skirt, may inflate those readings, and the report flags that doubt. Early results from this multi-phase study will shape recommendations for watching remedy performance across the site.
doe-osti-2999079-contact-retention-stren:
Steven DiGregorio, Laurie Burnham, Alex Coker and Bruce King of Sandia National Laboratories present these slides, SAND2025-12492R, on 30 September 2025, to a photovoltaic quality meeting. The subject is the small 4-millimetre plug connectors that join solar panels. Inside each plug, a metal contact must stay fully seated. If it creeps out of place, resistance, heat and failure risk all climb.

The team lists five ways contacts get displaced and reviews the locking designs meant to hold them. Early pull tests compare how much tensile force different connector models withstand. Field data sharpens the stakes: contacts seated outside the best insertion range, 8.5 millimetres plus or minus 1.5, were only 4.9 percent of the total, yet they accounted for 24.7 percent of critical failures. Repeated movement and withdrawal also wear retention down. The project goal is better standards and safer next-generation connectors.
doe-osti-3004187-infrared-cloud-imager-i:
N. Pust, C. McCann, A. Beard, and P. Nugent, all at NWB Sensors, compare instruments in ARM report DOE/SC-ARM-TR-326, dated November 2025. The instruments are infrared cloud imagers, which watch the sky in thermal infrared to map clouds day and night. The intercomparison checks how well the imager's cloud readings agree with established Atmospheric Radiation Measurement instruments at the Southern Great Plains site.

Reference data come from the atmospheric emitted radiance interferometer and from balloon-borne soundings, both long-running ARM data streams at the Lamont, Oklahoma site. Agreement matters because cloud fraction records feed climate analyses that span decades and instrument swaps. Vendor-run intercomparisons like this one give the ARM facility an independent check before an instrument joins or stays in the network. The report is part of the facility's technical report series.
doe-osti-3011591-california-bridge-to-th:
A traineeship linking California students to the future Electron Ion Collider is closed out in a final report by Zhongbo Kang of the University of California, Los Angeles, for grant DE-SC0022358. The programme partnered the California EIC Consortium with the Cal Bridge network across University of California, California State University, and community college campuses. The reporting period ran from January 2022 to August 2024.

Four students from CSU and Cal Poly campuses held research placements in theory, computation, and experiment. One project calculated particle production in the Color Glass Condensate framework. A hybrid working model handled the distance between students and UCLA mentors. Several trainees went on to graduate study in physics.
doe-osti-3011860-community-choice-aggreg:
Data collection for community choice aggregation programs is laid out in a July 2025 webinar deck by Sushmita Jena of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. The session supports the Status and Trends in the Voluntary Market Report with 2024 data. Voluntary renewable buying in 2023 reached about 9.7 million customers and 319 million megawatt hours, one in sixteen United States retail customers.

The collection form runs five pages across program, residential, non residential, and power source sections. Only sales above renewable portfolio standards count, meaning RECs retired solely for program members. Utility pricing programs also served about 1.3 million customers with 15.3 million megawatt hours in 2023.
doe-osti-3016086-analysis-of-persistent-:
Matthew Muller was the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5K00-98636, and Michael Valerino is also named on the record. The subject is persistent soiling, dirt that builds up on solar panels and does not wash off in rain. The eastern United States was the main study region.

The lab analyzed data from sensors and equipment supplied by the participant. The aim was to pin down how fast persistent films form and what causes them. The plan had been to compare airborne pollen levels and weather against the losses. Instead, the team found fungus was the main biological agent, which switched the research direction. The results feed the participant's predictive soiling model, so panel owners can forecast output losses that rain will not fix.
doe-osti-3017648-resilient-crop-producti:
Felix B Fritschi of the University of Missouri and Wendy H Yang of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign co-chaired the workshop behind this report, DOE/SC-2028. Sharon L Doty and five more scientists formed the writing team. The Resilient Bioenergy Crop Production Workshop met from October 30 to November 1, 2024. It belongs to a federal workshop series on frontier science for the bioeconomy.

The report sets out what resilient crop production requires, then maps knowledge gaps and research opportunities. Cover imagery shows biomass sorghum holding productivity under drought at an Illinois field station, aerial roots and all. Inside, topics run from soil microbes to plant control of nitrifiers around roots, which shifts the nitrogen balance fields depend on. The audience is the research community itself: the document is an agenda, naming the experiments and tools the field needs next to keep bioenergy crops productive under stress.
doe-osti-3055732-rockies-plains-energy-a:
Colorado State University and Innosphere Ventures ran the REACH accelerator under award DE-EE0009609, from October 2021 to June 2024, with Bryan Willson as project lead. REACH stands for Rockies Plains Energy Accelerator for Commercializing Hardtech. Hardtech means energy startups whose product is physical gear, not just software. Based in Fort Collins, the program recruited young firms across the Rockies and Plains and coached them toward market.

Cohort 1 took 13 teams and cohort 2 took 14, with extra seats paid by outside partners. A third grouping folded in two follow-on programs rather than a fresh class. Scorecards track new partners, 47 against a goal of 20 in one line, and report that 40 percent of third cohort firms support disadvantaged communities, matching the target.
doe-osti-3097332-reducing-randomized-qua: Yigit Subasi of Los Alamos National Laboratory presents a one-slide research highlight, LA-UR-26-23270, issued April 22, 2026. It covers cutting the cost of randomized quantum algorithms. His team derived the best sampling strategy for lowering total resource cost. Cost can mean gate counts, circuit depth, runtime, or even energy used. Importance sampling cuts resources for tasks such as probabilistic noise cancellation, with no tradeoff. The method was posted as a 2026 preprint with Davide Cugini and Touheed Anwar Atif.
doe-osti-3364291-low-cost-highly-recycla:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-39208, by Wenbin Kuang, Vishal Kumar, Dounia Boushab, Kevin L. Simmons, and Khaled W. Shahwan, dates to April 2026. It develops structural composites that car makers could recycle instead of landfilling. The material pairs basalt fiber, spun from volcanic rock, with vitrimer resin. That resin can be reshaped and repaired with heat, unlike ordinary thermosets. A pultrusion line pulls the fibers through resin to form long parts cheaply.

The background explains the stakes. Vitrimer composites can cut part weight by as much as 40 percent versus steel. Basalt carries roughly a tenth of carbon fiber's embodied energy. It also tolerates temperatures above 1000 degrees Celsius. Barriers are practical: vitrimers are new, and pultrusion is unproven in high-volume car production. The project builds the missing performance and cost knowledge.
doe-osti-3365148-technical-basis-savy-40:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-24149, by Timothy A. Stone, Jonah J. Newton, and Tristan M. Karns, builds the technical basis for the 5.5-gallon member of the SAVY-4000 nuclear material storage container family. The 5.5G keeps the proven design of the smaller quart-size containers but stretches the deep-drawn body wider and deeper for more volume. Containers storing nuclear material must survive drops and decades of service under DOE Manual 441.1-1.

Equivalency analysis, calculation, and test data argue that the 5.5G complies at a 9-foot drop height, rather than the 12 feet qualified for its smaller siblings, and that a 25-year design life is justified. The argument leans on the family's approval history, which began with a five-year life and grew through surveillance evidence.
doe-osti-3365386-novel-aqueous-geochemis:
A Johns Hopkins University final report for DOE award DE-SC0019830, led by Dimitri Sverjensky, models water, rock, and hydrocarbon chemistry at the extreme pressures and temperatures of Earth's deep interior. Experiments now reach 4.0 gigapascals and 400 degrees Celsius for salt solutions. The project tested whether geochemical equations of state predict fluid behavior there, and chased two puzzles: carbon dioxide chemistry at depth, and immiscible oil-water fluids seen at 3.0 gigapascals and 300 degrees.

Diamond inclusions delivered the surprise. Fluid models matched the chemistry of silicate inclusions trapped in diamonds worldwide, but the match implies the inclusions record the fluids that formed the diamonds, not the host rock as long assumed. Formate, an organic acid anion, also appears stable at upper mantle conditions, the first organic species besides hydrocarbons documented there.
doe-osti-3365719-measurements-of-tracer-:
University of Colorado Boulder's final report for DOE award DE-SC0021381, dated May 29, 2026 with Brian Argrow as technical contact, covers drone measurements for the TRACER campaign near Houston, Texas. Total project costs were 869,935 dollars, with the University of Oklahoma as partner. Two small unmanned aircraft, Colorado's RAAVEN and Oklahoma's CopterSonde, profiled the air before storms formed, south and southeast of the city near the Gulf coast sea breeze.

Flights built four-dimensional pictures of the boundary layer: temperature, humidity, winds, turbulent fluxes, and aerosol sizes from 150 to 2,500 nanometers. The CopterSonde flew as many as 19 sorties on busy June 2022 days at two sites. Quality-controlled data went to the DOE ARM archive for public use. The drone view complements the campaign's radar and lightning instruments by catching the pre-storm air they cannot sample.
doe-osti-3366033-upstream-extraction-of-:
5N Plus Inc.'s final report for DOE award DE-EE0011418, led by Frederic Belanger and covering calendar year 2025, develops a way to pull tellurium out of copper concentrates before smelting. Tellurium is a critical mineral for thin-film solar cells, and copper ore is its main source, yet smelters recover it late and inefficiently from anode slimes. The project was funded under a thin-film photovoltaics program.

Upstream extraction aims to capture tellurium at the concentrate stage, improving recovery and keeping it out of smelter waste streams. The report documents the process development work of the one-year project and its results for the solar program office. For a solar industry dependent on cadmium telluride panels, a domestic tellurium stream recovered earlier in the copper chain has clear supply value.
doe-osti-3373998-fitting-the-resrad-exte:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/EVS-26/11, dated June 2026, by E. K. Gnanapragasam, S. Kamboj, D. J. LePoire, and C. Yu fits the RESRAD dose model to a federal reference data set. RESRAD is Argonne's code for working out radiation doses at sites with leftover radioactive material. The reference is Federal Guidance Report 15, which tabulates external dose rate coefficients for radionuclides in air, water, and soil.

The team adjusts the RESRAD external dose rate model so its output matches the FGR 15 values across long lists of radionuclides. Page after page of tables gives the fitted values isotope by isotope, so RESRAD users can check their dose results against the federal numbers. A close fit means cleanup and risk studies built on RESRAD rest on the same footing as the national guidance.
doe-osti-3374762-tasti-grid-an-overview-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory letter report ORNL/LTR-2026/4374, by Hillary K. Fishler, Alexandra Kahl, and Varisara Tansakul, reviews grid resilience across Minnesota's counties and tribal lands. The data come from the lab's TASTI-GRID platform. The report is a planning overview, not a live monitoring tool. Some source data are incomplete, and the authors say so plainly.

For 2024, Minnesota logged a SAIFI of 1.262 interruptions per customer. Its SAIDI, the average minutes lost per customer, was 222.4 minutes with major event days counted. Against all states, Minnesota sits above the middle of the pack. It ranks twenty-first in impact level and twelfth in recovery duration. The longest recovery span ran about 415 minutes. Impact peaks in the Twin Cities metro counties, led by Hennepin and Ramsey.
doe-osti-3388185-requesting-an-exemption:
Requesting an Exemption from Standard Compliance is a July 2026 guidance document in the EPAct State and Alternative Fuel Provider Fleet Program. It tells covered fleets how to ask the Department of Energy to excuse an alternative fuel vehicle acquisition requirement. Exemptions rest on narrow bases. They include a lack of available alternative fuels and a lack of available alternative fuel vehicles. For state government entities only, unreasonable financial hardship is a third. The department reviews each request case by case.

Timing rules are strict. A fleet may file only after its annual report for the model year is submitted and approved. It may file only inside a window from September 1 following the model year to the next January 31. For model year 2030, that is September 1, 2030 through January 31, 2031. The guidance recommends filing through the online Compliance Reporting Tool. It also distinguishes exemptions from exclusions from the program.
doe-osti-3393363-e2c-successful-project-:
Joyce McLaren, a senior research analyst, presents the E2C Successful Project Implementation Cohort's overview of solar, microgrid, and resilience project development in slides dated February 2026. The cohort's participants named their needs up front. They were procurement, staff capacity, and working across internal and interagency lines. The session answers with process, broken into stages a local team can follow.

Solar development starts with scouting sites: roof type, age, and condition, and a building load review. System sizing against tariff limits, early utility coordination, and stakeholder engagement follow. Procurement comes next, choosing a development model, running a request for proposals, and selecting a developer. The deck warns that RFPs written too tight or too loose both fail. Proposals with different pricing structures are hard to compare. Permitting and development, microgrid technology types, and resilience hubs complete the day.
doe-osti-3422016-high-throughput-laser-p:
Report NLR/TP-5K00-99332 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated August 2026, pairs fast laser patterning with acoustic checks for battery making. Bertrand Tremolet de Villers and Donal Finegan were the lab contacts. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-20-17191.

Laser ablation cut fine structure into graphite electrode rolls. Treated rolls then went into prismatic lithium-ion batteries for tests. Roll-to-roll runs were tried at several process speeds. The team later summed up the scaling path in a published paper. Faster electrode patterning could lift battery charging speed without needing any new cell chemistry at all.
doe-osti-3584417-infrared-cloud-imager-i:
NWB Sensors sent its infrared cloud imager to the Southern Great Plains site in Oklahoma for a guest test. Report DOE/SC-ARM-26-031, dated August 2026, is by Nathan Pust, Cooper McCann, Austin Beard, and Paul Nugent, all at NWB Sensors. The run lasted from May 18 to December 12, 2023. Its main goal was to check the radiometric accuracy of the firm's full-sky cloud camera.

The imager records downwelling infrared light across the sky, day and night, and derives cloud products from it. Its readings were compared with a reference interferometer at the site. Two faults shaped the usable record: bird droppings fouled the reference mirror, and a lens cleaning on August 28 shifted the imager data. Only data after that cleaning are used in the study. Images and products were stored each minute and sent to the ARM Data Center.
doe-osti-3794254-selected-ion-spectrosco:
A final project report dated September 9, 2026 closes award DE-SC0018835 for Michael Duncan at the University of Georgia. The project ran from August 2018 to January 2026 under the Office of Basic Energy Sciences. It studied how uranium and thorium ions bind small molecules, stripped of solvents and salts. Bare ion clusters form in a laser-vaporized metal beam, chilled and sorted by mass. Laser light breaks chosen clusters apart, and the fragments reveal bond shapes and strengths.

Infrared tests probed nitrogen and carbon dioxide shells around uranium ions. Nitrogen filled its shell at eight ligands in a square antiprism shape. A doubly charged uranium oxide ion also took eight ligands, in a less symmetric frame. Colour-range light mapped excited states and break-off points, giving bond energies. A third rig images fragments to track how breakups unfold. Computer models with relativity built in run beside each test.
emma-mcchesney-and-co:
Edna Ferber's Emma McChesney and Co collects linked stories about Emma McChesney, star traveling saleswoman for the Buck Featherloom Petticoat Company, now a partner in the firm. The first chapter, Broadway to Buenos Aires, opens on the closed office door that means she is busy and T A Buck must wait. Her son Jock and her secretary Miss Morrissey recur throughout.

Emma sells petticoats, outtalks buyers, studies fashion in blue serge and hoops, and weighs business against her son's future. Ferber based her on real drummers she met as a young reporter, and Emma became one of her most loved creations. The stories mix comedy with respect for a woman who earns her standing order by order.
fascinating-san-francisco:
Brandt's Fascinating San Francisco is a love letter to the city in magazine form. Fred Brandt wrote the sketch, dated San Francisco 1924. Bret Harte's line, O Warder of Two Continents, fronts the piece. From Dana to Stevenson, from Harte to Mencken, admirers crowd its opening.

Kipling's dry verdict is quoted: the city's one drawback is that it is hard to leave. Brandt traces it from drowsy Spanish pueblo to child of the mines. Gold-spangled Argonaut days fed its growth, he writes. He calls it the most American yet most cosmopolitan place on the continent. Inez Haynes Irwin warns strangers to see California before entering it. Her joke warns that the city swallows all travel plans.
gaspar-the-gaucho-a-story-of-the-gran-ch:
Captain Mayne Reid opens his 1880 tale by mapping the Gran Chaco, a wild borderland of South America between the Salado, Paraná, and Paraguay rivers. Few outsiders knew the region then. Gaspar, a gaucho guide who knows its plains, rivers, and peoples, leads the party at the heart of the story. Ludwig and young Cypriano ride with him.

Flood, drought, and hostile bands turn a ride across the Chaco into a fight to stay alive. Gaspar reads signs in the land that his greener companions miss, as when a green plain turns overnight into a glittering sheet of water. Reid packs the tale with notes on plants, beasts, and native life. It suits readers who like frontier adventure mixed with natural history.
gold-sport-and-coffee-planting-in-mysore:
Robert H. Elliot spent thirty-eight years as a planter in Mysore, in southern India, and this 1898 book sums up the life. He had told part of it in 1871, in Experiences of a Planter in the Jungles of Mysore. The book is dedicated to Sir K. Sheshadri Iyer, Dewan of Mysore, whose rule Elliot praises. A map in colors goes with the text.

Gold mining, big-game sport, and coffee planting share the pages. Side chapters treat coffee in Coorg, the Mysore Representative Assembly, the Indian Congress, caste, and the silver question. Elliot writes as a practical man of the empire, proud of its order and keen on its profits. Modern readers will find his views of India dated, yet his detail on planting, sport, and rule is firsthand and rich.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AssassinationJF:
Who would control the Kennedy autopsy photographs and X-rays became a legal question within three years of the assassination. This file holds the correspondence and legal papers on their custody, including the 1966 letter agreement signed by Burke Marshall for the Kennedy estate's executors.

The papers also include the 1967 supplementary autopsy report, part of the effort to fix the medical record in official hands. The autopsy materials were deposited under restrictions that kept them from public view, which fed decades of dispute over the medical evidence. The file is the paper trail of that custody fight, kept complete for researchers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BantaCo_Banta_C:
Harold Weisberg published his assassination books himself, and self-publishing ran on paperwork like this. On July 21, 1975, the Collegiate Press division of the George Banta Company wrote to Weisberg quoting printing costs for a 672-page book.

The quotation prices the making of a fat research volume, the kind Weisberg produced in his Whitewash series, dense with reproduced government documents. His books reached readers outside commercial publishing and at his own expense, which is why a printer's quote sits in his files. The letter is a small record of how the assassination literature was physically made and paid for.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAMexico_CIA_M:
Philip Agee served the CIA in Latin America and resigned to write Inside the Company: CIA Diary, the 1975 book that named agency officers and operations wholesale. This memorandum, dated January 15, 1967, on the CIA's Mexico City officers comes from that book.

Mexico City station mattered out of proportion to its size: Lee Harvey Oswald visited the city in the fall of 1963, and its officers covered the Cuban and Soviet embassies he contacted. Agee's diary method was to print the personnel and the paperwork together. The memo survives in researchers' files as part of the record his disclosures created.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Counter-revolut:
Fenton Wheeler's wire story reports a startling claim from Havana. Anti-Castro commandos captured by Cuban forces told a news conference there that they had carried bullets tipped with potassium cyanide. Their target, they said, was Fidel Castro himself, and they described the plan openly once they were in custody.

The story records the plot as the captured men described it, in their own setting and on the record. Reports like this one show how the fight against Castro's government was waged in this period: small armed groups, secret landings, and assassination plans stated openly once the men were caught.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DallasCountyJai:
On November 1, 1979, Harold Weisberg wrote a memorandum about seventeen prisoners held in the Dallas County jail. The men reportedly witnessed the assassination of President Kennedy. According to Weisberg, the FBI never interviewed them, despite what they might have seen.

The memo also examines how the Bureau handled the tip that pointed to these witnesses. For Weisberg, the episode fit a pattern: leads near the scene went unchecked while the official account hardened. His memorandum preserves the names and the paper trail of the complaint, so later readers can judge the missed interviews for themselves.
in-morocco:
Edith Wharton traveled through Morocco in 1918 and published In Morocco in 1920. She thanks General Lyautey and his wife, whose kindness made the trip she had long dreamed of. Wharton notes that Morocco still lacked a guide-book when she went. War made the sea trip from Marseilles slow and hard.

Rain set the limit, since trails in the Spanish zone turn treacherous. She reached Tangier by land before the November rains. Pages describe Fez, palm oases, reservoirs, and a sultan's pleasure house called the Menara. Her eye for place and custom is sharp and clear.
life-and-labors-of-elder-john-kline-the-:
Benjamin Funk collated this life of Elder John Kline from Kline's diary. The Brethren Publishing House at Elgin, Illinois, issued it in 1900. Kline was a German Baptist elder in Rockingham County, Virginia. His grave slab stands in the Linville's Creek church burying ground.

The introduction reflects on whether the dead live on beyond the grave. It argues, from nature and Scripture, that death is not life's end. Kline's own diary then grounds the story of his labors. Church readers know him by the title the book gives: martyr missionary. The Brethren Publishing House at Elgin, Illinois, printed the diary-based life in 1900.
life-in-mexico:
Frances Calderón de la Barca wrote these letters from Mexico. She was born in Edinburgh in 1804, daughter of William Inglis. After her father's death she settled in America. There she married Spanish diplomat Don Angel Calderón de la Barca.

She accompanied him on appointments to Mexico, Washington, and Madrid. Her Mexican residence lasted two years, with Prescott prefacing the book. The Everyman's Library edition made her letters a travel classic. Alfonso XII later created her Marquesa, and she died in 1882. Harper published her conquest history reference in New York in 1843. The Attaché in Madrid followed from her later Spanish years.
mcteague-a-story-of-san-francisco:
Frank Norris set McTeague, a story of San Francisco, on Polk Street. Chapter one shows the dentist on a Sunday, his one day of ease. He dines at two at a car conductors' coffee joint.

Back in his Dental Parlors, he drinks steam beer and plays the concertina. His canary sings in a gilt cage above his head. The music takes him back to the Big Dipper Mine in Placer County. There his father bossed shifts, and his mother cooked for forty miners. He knew just six sad airs, and played them each week. Norris builds a whole man from habit, food, and small joys.
modern-french-philosophy-a-study-of-the-:
J. Alexander Gunn, a fellow of the University of Liverpool, published this study in 1922. Henri Bergson, France's most famous living philosopher, supplied the foreword. Gunn traces French philosophy from its antecedents through the main currents since 1851. Comte and positivism stand behind that starting date.

Chapters take up science, freedom, progress, ethics, and religion in turn. A bibliography, comparative table, and index close the book. Gunn lectured in psychology for the Liverpool extension board, and writes for students. His survey gave English readers a map of French thought in the generation after Comte, written while Bergson's own influence was at its height.
morocco:
A. S. Forrest painted the pictures for this travel volume, and S. L. Bensusan described the journey. Adam and Charles Black published it in London in 1904. The motto, from Eothen, reads: as I have felt, so I have written. The contents start by Cape Spartel, at Africa's northwestern corner.

The travelers ride from Tangier to Djedida, then take the Moorish road. The road leads to the gates of Marrakesh, and into red Marrakesh itself. Bensusan writes text to match Forrest's paintings of markets, roads, and walls. Such painted travel books let Edwardian readers tour a Morocco still closed to most Europeans.
nasa-tm-19650003004-electronically-steer:
Dennis L Backus of Goddard Space Flight Center presented this work in September 1964 in Washington. His subject was antennas for communication satellites that steer their beam with electronics, not with motors or moving dishes.

Backus reviews several steering methods for use roughly between one and three and a half gigacycles. He argues such antennas could be built to give strong gain for their weight and wide bandwidth. They could also light up chosen areas on the ground. The paper shows an early path away from heavy, moving satellite antennas. That promise mattered, because a beam that moves without moving parts has far less that can fail in orbit.
nasa-tm-19650025629-the-latitudinal-dist:
Television pictures from the TIROS III weather satellite, analyzed by computer, form the base of this study from the Goddard Institute for Space Studies and New York University. The authors map how cloud cover is spread by latitude, from equator to poles. Their data cover the summer of 1961, an early season for weather satellites.

Cloud cover by latitude is a basic fact about Earth's climate. Before satellites, no one could see the whole pattern at once. A computer did the counting across many photographs. The result gave meteorologists a global picture they had never had, and a base line against which later satellite records could be compared.
nasa-tm-19670015307-procedures-for-exter:
T. S. Humphries, of the Propulsion and Vehicle Engineering Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote these procedures on June 29, 1966. Numbered TM X-53483, they govern how to load metal test specimens from outside and then expose them to corrosion. The target failure mode is stress corrosion cracking, where a stressed metal cracks in a corrosive setting.

Humphries describes the specimen types in detail: threaded-end round tensile pieces, flat tensile pieces, bent beam specimens, and C-ring specimens. Preparation steps and test environments are specified for each. The accelerated corrosion test alternates immersion in a salt solution of three and a half percent sodium chloride. The procedures had proven reliable for evaluating most aluminum alloys, the abstract reports, and showed promise for ferrous and nickel alloys as well.
nasa-tm-19680019095-research-achievement:
Marshall Space Flight Center's Research Achievements Review, volume 2, covers computation research at the center, in a 1967 memorandum, TM X-53724. Computing at Marshall then centered on a Univac 1108, described as a third generation machine. The volume surveys how the center ran that system and what its engineers built around it.

Chapters cover daily computer operations and languages shaped for engineering problems, stated in shapes and in geometry. Other sections treat information retrieval systems and computers carried aboard spacecraft. Remote stations with teletypes and display screens gave many users quick access at once. Figures show graphics work, circuit design, flight path problems, and structural design done on the machine.
nasa-tm-19680019448-nonlinear-time-domai:
Lawrence W. Taylor Jr. of NASA's Flight Research Center presented this paper on human controller models at a Honolulu conference in January 1968. Control systems with a human in the loop need a math model of the human's control behavior. Since Tustin's 1947 tracking work, many researchers have built such models from experiment data.

Most earlier models were linear and built in the frequency domain. Taylor examines nonlinear, time-domain analysis for the same problem. In tracking tests, a pilot works a controller to keep a displayed error near zero. Recorded signals then reveal the pilot's response pattern. Time-domain methods may capture how pilots adapt as aircraft dynamics change.
nasa-tm-19690027199-research-achievement:
Communication and tracking research fills volume 3 of Marshall's Research Achievements Review, in a 1968 memorandum, TM X-53810. Marshall's teams were then pushing beyond radio toward light itself for spacecraft links. The volume opens with recent advances in pointing and tracking instrumentation at the center.

One study weighs the data rates attainable with optical and infrared communications. Diagrams show a laser communication system and its telescope, tracking a simulated Earth beacon. Charts report measured detection performance and error rates against receiver size. John M. Gould then presents laser pointing, tracking, and ranging work. His sections cover a target motion estimator, the range servo, and the angular control system.
nasa-tm-19700024253-apollo-mcc-msfn-miss:
Staff at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this system description in March 1970. It covers the mission configuration for the AS-508 Apollo flight. AS-508 was the vehicle for the Apollo 13 mission.

The document lays out how the Mission Control Center and the Manned Space Flight Network were set up. It covers command, communication, telemetry, and tracking for the mission. Ground stations around the world had to pass voice and data to Houston without gaps. Configuration records like this one fixed who did what, and with what gear, before the flight began.
nasa-tm-19710003420-conceptual-design-of:
