James J. Ward, Roland Breitwieser, and Richard M. Williams of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an October 1970 conference in Miami. It gives a concept design for a nuclear thermionic power system. The converters that turn heat into power sit outside the reactor core.

The team took a fresh look at this layout in light of recent gains. New alloys stand heat and corrosion better, and heat pipes now carry far more heat. Converters had improved, and light radiators could cool the system. They then studied what changes when the design is scaled down. The target size was a mid-range plant for space power.
nasa-tm-19710013148-longitude-reposition:
Thomas A O'Malley of the Lewis Research Center wrote this April 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2258. It studies how to move a large communications satellite to a new longitude. The satellite stays in synchronous equatorial orbit, circling once per day. Operators may need such a move when traffic or coverage plans change.

O'Malley showed that fuel needs depend on three things. They are the size of the longitude change, the allowed travel time, and the push the propulsion system gives. Low thrust electric propulsion may need to fire across many orbits to finish the move. The analysis gave planners a way to budget fuel and time for repositioning.
nasa-tm-19710013890-magnetic-storm-effec:
H. G. Mayr and H. Volland wrote this NASA preprint, numbered X-621-71-141, on what magnetic storms do to the neutral air high above Earth. Their focus is the thermosphere, where storm heating in the auroral zone sets winds in motion. The paper asks how those winds change the mix of gases that satellites fly through.

The authors show that the storm-driven wind circulation can sweep atomic oxygen away from high latitudes. Near about one hundred eighty kilometers up, the oxygen density can fall by as much as half. That drop matches storm-time changes seen in the ionosphere. Higher up, thermal expansion cancels the effect, which explains why oxygen barely changes there even while molecular nitrogen rises sharply.
parrot-co: The hosted sample shows only the front matter of Parrot & Co., the title pages and table of contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Harold MacGrath as the author and lists his earlier novels, The Best Man and The Carpet from Bagdad. The book was copyrighted in 1913 by the Bobbs-Merrill Company, issued in New York by A. L. Burt, and carried four colour illustrations by André Castaigne.
stalky-co: Rudyard Kipling heads Stalky and Co. with a long verse in praise of famous men. Men of little showing, the verse says, whose work goes on greater than their knowing. Western wind and open surge tore the boys from their mothers and flung them on a naked shore, twelve bleak houses by the shore, amid two hundred brothers. There they met the famous men set in office over them, who beat them with rods daily, faithfully, for the love they bore them.
the-city-that-was-a-requiem-of-old-san-f:
Will Irwin wrote this requiem for old San Francisco as a newspaper piece for The Sun, published April 21, 1906. That date falls three days after the disaster that struck the city. The piece is recast here as a book, by special permission of The Sun, and Irwin credits Franklin Matthews for its title.

His opening verdict is plain: the old San Francisco is dead. He mourns a city he calls the gayest and most pleasure loving on the western continent, and in many ways its most romantic. Its people now live as refugees among ruins. It may rebuild, and probably will, but it can never be the same. He compares the city to a pretty, frivolous woman who has passed through tragedy and survives sobered and changed. The hills of the Coast Range, he adds, framed that lost city.
the-legends-of-san-francisco: George W. Caldwell, a physician and author of legends of Southern California, dedicates his San Francisco verse to the Native Daughters of California. Only the dedication poem and contents are present here, praising seven hills, fog, sea air, and tireless city energy. The contents list four pieces on the Maid of Tamalpais, twin guardians of the Golden Gate, sea gulls, and islands of the bay. The legend poems themselves are absent from this record.
the-story-of-crisco: The Procter and Gamble Company of Cincinnati issued this cookbook, here in an eleventh edition priced at twenty-five cents, to tell the story of its Crisco shortening. Only the title pages and table of contents are present here. The contents promise advice on choosing foods. Methods and time tables for cooking follow. The art of carving comes next. Recipe sections then cover many dishes. Soups, fish, and meats come first. Vegetables, salads, and puddings follow. Sandwiches, pastries, and breads close the list. The recipes themselves do not appear.
the-white-chief-a-legend-of-northern-mex:
Captain Mayne Reid subtitled The White Chief a legend of northern Mexico, in a printing dated 1855. Chapter one climbs with the reader to the snowy summit of the Sierra Blanca, the hunter's Spanish Peaks, deep in the continent's interior. Mountains crowd the north, south, and west for thousands of miles, while eastward a plain runs a thousand miles without a single mountain.

Through a telescope, settlements of Nuevo Mexico glint along the Rio del Norte, but the story lies east, below the peak. A lovely valley, San Ildefonso, spreads ten miles between thousand-foot cliffs, watered by a winding silver stream. Deer and elk roam it now, yet a companion points out ruins near its centre: a city once stood in this wild paradise.
through-the-grand-canyon-from-wyoming-to: E. L. Kolb wrote an account of travelling through the Grand Canyon from Wyoming to Mexico, published by Macmillan at New York in a 1915 new edition. Owen Wister supplied a foreword. Seventy-two plates reproduce photographs by Kolb and his brother. A frontispiece shows the canyon at the mouth of Havasu Creek, credited to the Kolb brothers. Copyright dates place the first edition in 1914, reprinted the next year. The title and publication pages are what is shown in this record, so Kolb's river journey itself does not appear.
tommy-and-co:
Jerome K. Jerome's Tommy and Co., published by Hutchinson at London in 1904, opens with its first story, Peter Hope plans his prospectus. Peter Hope is tall, thin, and clean-shaven except for close side whiskers, with hair thinning on top. His white but frayed linen asserts itself against a retiring cut-away coat.

Jerome lingers on the coat's wish to slip off its owner's back, the black silk cravat held by chained gold pins, and strapped grey trousers under the table. A small white face with bright black eyes peers round the door. Readers get Jerome's comic portraiture of an ageing, shabby-genteel editor.
travels-through-the-empire-of-morocco:
John Buffa, a physician to the forces, explains in his 1810 preface how a Gibraltar posting sent him into Morocco. He had been placed on half-pay in June 1805 after service at the Isle of Wight depot hospital. A quarantine medical post at Gibraltar was proposed for him, backed by the Duke of Kent.

Buffa reached Gibraltar and waited months for a commission that never came. Then the British consul general at Tangier asked him to cross to Barbary. His patient was the governor of Larache, first minister of the emperor. The travels that follow grew from that medical errand, and a map of the empire accompanies the book.
vignettes-of-san-francisco: Almira Bailey wrote Vignettes of San Francisco, a set of city sketches. Pages shown here hold the title page and a list of the pieces only, so the sketches themselves are not shown. Titles wander the whole city. They name the ferry, the Union-Street car, and Market-Street scintillations. Cafeterias, the open board of trade, Fillmore Street, and Portsmouth Square follow. The lobby of the St. Francis, Golden Gate Park, and the fog in San Francisco close the list. Another tells of the garbage-man's little girl.
when-valmond-came-to-pontiac-the-story-o:
Gilbert Parker called When Valmond Came to Pontiac a historical fantasy in his introduction. He ranks it apart from all his other books. It came out in the summer of 1895, between two of his other Canadian tales. Critics praised it warmly, which both pleased and daunted him. One paper said it read as if written at a single sitting.

Parker admits that paper was nearly right. He wrote, printed, and revised the book in five weeks. The draft took four weeks of night and day work at Hot Springs, Virginia. Valmond, a lost Napoleon figure, comes to a French Canadian village and stirs old loyalties. Speed of making matches the tale's fevered charm.
widger-s-quotations-from-project-gutenbe: Nothing beyond a Project Gutenberg header appears here, so Widger's chosen lines from Rousseau are absent. The header names the source as The Confessions of J. J. Rousseau. David Widger's set is number 15 in his Quotations series. It was released in February 2003 as etext number 3749. The first posting date given is August 19, 2001, with edition 10 named. Standard notes on copyright, donations, and file keeping fill the rest of the header.
